Limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) is the test for carbon(IV) oxide, turning milky. That same solution neutralises acidic gases and softens water.
The test for Ca²⁺ is a brick-red flame colour. Calcium ions give that colour in a flame test, confirming the ion in any mixture.
Calcium carbonate also neutralises acidic soils in the field and builds reefs in the sea. One compound, three industries.
bullets: CaO: cement, steel-making, soil neutralisation.
Ca(OH)₂: mortar, water treatment; limewater tests CO₂.
Ca²⁺ flame test: brick red.
content.takeaway: The three calcium compounds feed building, soil treatment and tests.

check.question: The flame colour of calcium ions is
check.why: Calcium gives a brick-red flame — its specific test.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For calcium items, follow the chain in order: carbonate heated to oxide, oxide slaked to hydroxide. The preparation names the process each time.

content.problem: Sea shells (calcium carbonate) are heated to make quicklime. Write the equation and state the gas released.

steps.reason: Sea shells are calcium carbonate (CaCO₃)
Heating decomposes the carbonate to the oxide and carbon dioxide
The carbon leaves as its oxide

content.question: Quicklime (CaO) is slaked with water. Write the equation and name the product.
hints: Slaking adds water to the oxide

content.heading: Go deeper: Why cement needs gypsum
paragraphs: Gypsum is ground with clinker to make cement, and without it the cement would set almost instantly. Tricalcium aluminate reacts with water too fast, and gypsum slows it by forming a protective layer that controls the pace.
That controlled pace is what building trades need: enough working time to place the mortar, then a predictable hardening. Gypsum is therefore not a filler but a regulator.
The setting time also depends on fineness: finer cement hydrates faster and sets sooner. Grinding is part of the chemistry of speed.
A candidate who links gypsum to aluminate control understands cement manufacture as managed hydration, not just heating.
Without gypsum, the first water on cement would trigger a flash set — the mix would harden in minutes, long before it could be placed. The gypsum layer buys the working time the trade needs.
That window is measured in minutes and hours, and it is the reason cement is ground with gypsum in the mill rather than added on site. Control is built into the powder.
A candidate who names aluminate control as the role of gypsum has explained the only reason it is there. Anything else — strength, colour, cheapness — is decoration.
bullets: Gypsum slows tricalcium aluminate hydration.
Working time is the product; speed is the risk.
Finer cement sets faster; grinding controls speed.
Cement manufacture is managed hydration.

content.heading: Go deeper: Curing concrete
paragraphs: Hydration needs water throughout the hardening period, so new concrete is kept wet — covered or sprayed — for days. Dried-out concrete stops gaining strength because the reaction stops.
That is why curing is specified on building sites: the chemistry continues long after the pour, and strength is built in the second and third weeks, not the first day.
The same logic explains why mortar mixed too dry never reaches strength: the silicates have no water left to react with. Water is a reactant in setting, not just a mixer.
A candidate who treats curing as watering understands that concrete is still reacting weeks after it looks finished.
The strength gain follows the hydration curve: fast in the first days, then slower for weeks. That is why tests are run at 7 and 28 days, not on the day of the pour.
Mass concrete faces the opposite problem: hydration heat builds up inside, so large pours need cooling. The same reaction that strengthens can crack if its heat has nowhere to go.
bullets: Hydration needs water for days — keep concrete wet.
Strength builds in weeks, not on day one.
Water is a reactant, not just a mixer.
Dry concrete stops reacting and stays weak.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in calcium chemistry
paragraphs: The classic trap is the setting mechanism. Mortar sets by hydration (reaction with water), not by drying. Any option describing evaporation or air exposure misnames the process.
The second trap is the flame colour. Calcium is brick red, sodium golden yellow, potassium lilac. Swapping them reverses the identification.
The third trap is the order of the chain. Carbonate heated gives oxide; oxide plus water gives hydroxide. Reversing the order writes an impossible preparation.
The fourth trap is gypsum's role. It is a regulator of setting time, not a main component or a filler. Naming it as the setting agent reverses its function.

A final trap is calling limewater a base only. Limewater is calcium hydroxide solution, and its milky test with CO₂ is a precipitation of CaCO₃. The base and the test reagent are the same solution used two ways.
bullets: Setting = hydration, not drying.
Ca²⁺ flame is brick red.
Carbonate → oxide by heat; oxide + water → hydroxide.
Gypsum regulates setting time.

lessons.title: Aluminium and Tin
lessons.objective: Specify the method of purification of bauxite, the electrolytic extraction of aluminium, the properties and uses of aluminium and its compounds, and determine the test for Al³⁺; specify the ores of tin, relate the method of extraction to its properties, and specify the uses of tin.

content.heading: Aluminium and Tin
paragraphs: A cooking pot that does not rust and a food tin that seals tight are both made from metals pulled out of rock by electricity and fire. This lesson follows aluminium from its ore to its tests, and tin from its ore to its uses.

content.heading: Aluminium: purification and extraction
paragraphs: Bauxite is the ore of aluminium, a reddish rock rich in aluminium oxide. It is purified by the Bayer process: the oxide dissolves in hot concentrated NaOH, impurities are filtered off, and pure aluminium oxide precipitates and is calcined. That pure oxide is called alumina.

Alumina is electrolysed dissolved in cryolite (Na₃AlF₆), which lowers its melting point and saves energy. At the cathode, aluminium ions gain electrons and deposit as metal; at the carbon anode, oxide ions discharge as oxygen, which burns the anode away.

Aluminium sits high in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot reduce it — only electrolysis wins its electrons. Its extraction is therefore electricity-hungry, which is why aluminium is made near cheap power.
bullets: Bayer process purifies bauxite to alumina.
Alumina electrolysed in cryolite; oxygen burns the anode.
Aluminium needs electrolysis because it sits high in the series.
content.takeaway: Bauxite is purified to alumina, and alumina is electrolysed in cryolite.

check.question: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis rather than carbon reduction because
options: It is too reactive for carbon to displace it
It melts at too low a temperature
It does not occur in nature
check.why: Aluminium sits high in the series; carbon cannot pull its electrons away.

content.heading: Properties, uses and the test for Al³⁺
paragraphs: Aluminium is light (density one-third of iron), does not rust because its oxide film seals it, conducts well, and is malleable. Those four properties explain its uses: aircraft bodies, cooking pots, overhead cables and foil.

Its compounds include aluminium oxide (the abrasive itself), aluminium chloride and aluminium sulfate (used in water treatment). The oxide film is amphoteric: it reacts with both acids and bases, which is why aluminium dissolves in both.

The test for Al³⁺ is sodium hydroxide solution, which gives a white gelatinous precipitate of Al(OH)₃ that dissolves in excess NaOH. That double behaviour — precipitate, then dissolve — is specific to aluminium.
bullets: Light, rust-proof (oxide film), conducting, malleable.
Uses: aircraft, pots, cables, foil.
Al³⁺ test: white gelatinous precipitate with NaOH, soluble in excess.
content.takeaway: Aluminium's oxide film makes it light, rust-proof and useful — and Al³⁺ precipitates white with NaOH.

check.question: The test for Al³⁺ with sodium hydroxide solution gives
options: A white gelatinous precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH
check.why: Al(OH)₃ is white and gelatinous, and it dissolves in excess alkali.

content.heading: Tin: ore, extraction and uses
paragraphs: Tin is mined from cassiterite ore (SnO₂). The ore is concentrated by gravity because cassiterite is dense, then reduced with carbon in a furnace: SnO₂ + C → Sn + CO₂. Carbon works because tin sits low in the reactivity series.

Tin is a soft, silvery metal that resists corrosion and is used to coat iron (tin plate for food cans), in alloys like soft solder and bronze, and in some electrical work. Tin plate protects because tin forms a barrier — but as the earlier lesson showed, a scratched coating lets iron rust faster.
Tin's uses follow its properties: low melting point for soldering, corrosion resistance for coating, and softness for alloying. Each use is a property read off the metal.
bullets: Ore: cassiterite (SnO₂); extraction by carbon reduction.
Uses: tin plate, soft solder, bronze, electrical work.
Scratched tin plate accelerates rusting of iron.
content.takeaway: Tin comes from cassiterite by carbon reduction and coats iron against rust.

check.question: Tin is extracted from cassiterite by
check.why: Tin sits low in the series, so carbon displaces it from its oxide.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For extraction questions, locate the metal in the series first. The position names the method — electrolysis, carbon, or found free — every time.

content.problem: Alumina is electrolysed in cryolite. At which electrode does aluminium form, and why not carbon reduction?

steps.reason: Aluminium sits above zinc and iron
steps.result: Al is above Zn and Fe

steps.reason: Carbon cannot displace a metal above zinc
Metal ions gain electrons at the cathode

content.question: Tin is extracted by carbon reduction. What does that tell you about tin's position in the series?
hints: Carbon displaces only metals below zinc
Tin is extracted this way, so tin sits below zinc
The series position is the explanation

content.heading: Go deeper: Why cryolite is there
paragraphs: Aluminium oxide melts above 2000 °C, far too hot for an economical cell. Cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) dissolves alumina and drops the melting point to about 950 °C. That single addition makes the whole industry affordable.
Cryolite also conducts, which alumina alone does not. The electrolyte needs the salt for both melting point and conductivity — one mineral doing two jobs.
The anode is consumed because the oxygen released burns carbon to carbon dioxide. Anodes are therefore replaced regularly, a running cost unique to aluminium smelting.
A candidate who names cryolite's two jobs — melting point and conductivity — has explained the cell completely.
The cryolite also protects the cell lining from the corrosive melt, extending the furnace life. One mineral thus serves melting point, conductivity and furnace protection together.
A candidate who lists all three jobs has shown the complete picture; most answers name only the melting point.
The cells run day and night because stopping them would freeze the bath. Aluminium smelting is therefore a continuous process anchored to cheap electricity more than to any other input.
That continuity is also why aluminium recycling needs only a twentieth of the energy: melting scrap avoids the whole extraction chain.
bullets: Cryolite drops alumina melting point to ~950 °C.
Cryolite also conducts — two jobs, one mineral.
Released oxygen burns the carbon anode.
Anodes are replaced regularly in smelting.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why aluminium does not rust
paragraphs: Aluminium's oxide film is thin, transparent and self-healing: scratch it and the metal underneath oxidises again to seal the scratch. That self-repair is why pots and aircraft skins last for decades in rain.
The film is amphoteric — it dissolves in both acids and bases — which is why aluminium cookware is attacked by strong alkalis and why aluminium dissolves in both HCl and NaOH.
Iron's rust, by contrast, is porous and does not seal. Aluminium protects itself; iron does not. That single difference explains the durability of two metals in the same rain.
The exam contrast is therefore structural: a sealing film versus a non-sealing one. Naming the film is naming the explanation.
Anodising thickens that film deliberately by electrolysing aluminium in an acid bath, growing a harder, coloured coating used on cooking pots and aircraft parts.
The film logic also explains aluminium foil: it seals the food inside from air and moisture the same way it seals the metal from rust.
bullets: Aluminium oxide film seals scratches by re-oxidising.
The film is amphoteric (reacts with acids and bases).
Iron rust is porous and never seals.
Sealing film vs non-sealing rust decides durability.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in aluminium and tin
paragraphs: The classic trap is the bauxite step. The Bayer process purifies bauxite to alumina; electrolysis extracts the metal from alumina. Naming electrolysis as the purification reverses the factory order.
The second trap is the anode. Released oxygen burns the carbon anode, so the anode shrinks during electrolysis. Any option claiming the anode is inert is false.
The third trap is tin's protection. Tin plate barriers iron, but scratched tin accelerates rusting because iron becomes the anode. The coating protects only while whole.
The fourth trap is the Al³⁺ test direction. The precipitate dissolves in excess NaOH — the two-step behaviour separates aluminium from iron(III), whose precipitate does not dissolve.
A final trap is the extraction of tin. Cassiterite reduction uses carbon because tin sits below zinc in the series; any option giving electrolysis for tin reverses the series logic.
bullets: Bayer purifies; electrolysis extracts — do not reverse them.
The carbon anode burns away in the cell.
Scratched tin accelerates iron rusting.
Al(OH)₃ dissolves in excess NaOH; Fe(OH)₃ does not.

lessons.title: Iron and Steel
lessons.objective: Determine the suitable method of extraction of iron, specify its properties and uses, identify the different forms of iron with their compositions, properties and uses, and determine the specific tests for Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺.

content.heading: Iron and Steel
paragraphs: A gate, a bridge and a car body all begin as rusty rock in a furnace. This lesson follows iron from its ore to the steel that shapes the modern world.

content.heading: Extracting iron in the blast furnace
paragraphs: Iron is extracted from haematite ore (Fe₂O₃) by carbon reduction in a blast furnace. The furnace is charged with ore, limestone and coke, and hot air is blown in from the bottom. The coke burns to carbon monoxide, which reduces the oxide: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.
Limestone is the flux: it combines with the sandy impurities to form slag, which floats on the molten iron and is tapped off separately. That is why slag is a useful by-product, not waste.
Molten iron collects at the bottom and is tapped into moulds. It is run into ingots or taken straight to the steel converters.
bullets: Ore: haematite (Fe₂O₃); charge: ore + limestone + coke.
CO reduces the oxide; limestone forms slag with impurities.
Molten iron tapped at the bottom.
content.takeaway: Carbon monoxide reduces the ore; limestone flux carries the impurities away as slag.

check.question: In the blast furnace, the actual reducing agent is
check.why: Coke burns to CO, and CO reduces the iron oxide.

content.heading: Forms of iron and the making of steel
paragraphs: Pig iron is the crude blast-furnace product, rich in carbon (about 4%) and brittle. Wrought iron is nearly pure iron, soft and tough, made by puddling. Cast iron has less carbon than pig iron and is hard but brittle.
Steel is iron with a controlled small amount of carbon. Stainless steel adds chromium and nickel for rust resistance. The carbon content decides the type: more carbon means harder, stronger steel.
Steel is made by blowing oxygen through molten pig iron (basic oxygen furnace), which burns away excess carbon and impurities. The controlled burn is the difference between pig iron and steel.
bullets: Pig iron: ~4% C, brittle. Wrought iron: nearly pure, tough.
Cast iron: hard, brittle. Steel: controlled carbon.
Steel: oxygen burns excess carbon from pig iron.
content.takeaway: Carbon content separates pig iron, cast iron, wrought iron and steel.

check.question: Steel differs from pig iron in that
options: Its carbon content is controlled and lower
It is made from pure iron
It contains no impurities at all
check.why: Steel is pig iron with its carbon burnt down to a controlled level.

content.heading: Properties, uses and the tests for Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺
paragraphs: Iron is a grey, magnetic, conducting metal used for gates, beams, tools, machines and vehicles. Its weakness is rusting, which is why it is painted, galvanised or alloyed into steel.

The test for Fe²⁺ is potassium hexacyanoferrate(III) solution, which gives a deep blue precipitate (Prussian blue). The test for Fe³⁺ is potassium hexacyanoferrate(II), which also gives a blue precipitate — the reagents are swapped in the two tests.
With sodium hydroxide, Fe²⁺ gives a dirty green precipitate and Fe³⁺ gives a reddish-brown one. The two ions are therefore separable by their precipitate colours as well as by the blue tests.
bullets: Uses: construction, tools, machines, vehicles.
Fe²⁺: Prussian blue with hexacyanoferrate(III); dirty green with NaOH.
Fe³⁺: Prussian blue with hexacyanoferrate(II); reddish-brown with NaOH.
content.takeaway: Iron's weakness is rust; its two ions give two blue tests and two precipitate colours.

check.question: The test for Fe³⁺ uses
check.why: Fe³⁺ with hexacyanoferrate(II) gives Prussian blue; the reagent is the other iron complex.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For blast furnace items, always separate the three jobs: coke burns, carbon monoxide reduces, limestone fluxes. Mixing them loses the mark.

content.problem: In the blast furnace, haematite is reduced by carbon monoxide. Write the equation for Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe + CO₂.

steps.reason: Two irons on the left need two on the right
Three oxygens on the left must all appear in CO₂
Three carbons and three oxygens each side

content.question: Why is limestone added to the blast furnace charge? Give its chemical role.
hints: Impurities in the ore are sandy (silicon dioxide)
Limestone reacts with the sand to form slag
Slag floats on the iron and is tapped off

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the furnace is a blast furnace
paragraphs: The name comes from the blast: hot air is forced in at the bottom, and the rising gases meet the descending charge in counter-current. That arrangement maximises contact between gas and solid, which is why the furnace is tall and narrow.

The temperature also grades from bottom to top: hottest near the blast, cooler at the mouth. Different furnace zones do different jobs — drying at the top, reduction in the middle, melting at the bottom.
The slag is molten throughout, floating because it is less dense than iron. Two liquids tapped separately is the whole separation, driven by density alone.
A candidate who pictures the counter-current flow and the two liquids understands the furnace as a machine, not a list of facts.
The rising hot gases also preheat and dry the incoming charge, so the furnace recovers its own heat. That counter-current economy is what makes the process continuous rather than batch.
A candidate who traces the gases upward and the charge downward sees why the furnace can run for years without stopping.
bullets: Blast = hot air forced in; counter-current maximises contact.
Temperature grades bottom (hottest) to top (driest).
Slag floats on iron — two liquids, tapped separately.
The furnace is a machine, not a list.

content.heading: Go deeper: Carbon decides the form of iron
paragraphs: Pure iron (wrought iron) is soft and tough because its crystals slide past each other. Adding carbon pins those slides: more carbon means harder and stronger, up to a point, then brittle. Pig iron at 4% carbon is brittle precisely because the pinning is total.
Steelmakers live on that curve: mild steel (under 0.3% carbon) for beams and bodywork, high-carbon steel for tools and springs. Strength and brittleness are traded along one axis.
Stainless steel adds chromium, whose oxide film protects like aluminium's. The same film logic that saves aluminium saves stainless steel — different metal, same chemistry.
The exam chain is therefore: carbon content → properties → use. Naming the carbon percentage is naming the form.
The same curve explains why pure iron was forged for centuries before steel: without controlled carbon, the smith could only choose between soft wrought iron and brittle cast iron.
Modern steelmaking is therefore carbon management — burning exactly the right amount down from pig iron. The oxygen lance in a converter is a carbon-removal tool, not a purifier in general.
bullets: Pure iron is soft; carbon pins crystal slides.
Mild steel (<0.3% C) for beams; high-carbon for tools.
Stainless steel's chromium film resists rust like aluminium.
Carbon percentage names the form.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in iron chemistry
paragraphs: The classic trap is the reducing agent. Coke burns, but carbon monoxide reduces the ore. Any option naming carbon as the reducer reverses the furnace's chemistry.
The second trap is limestone's role. Limestone is a flux forming slag, not a fuel and not a reducer. Burning is coke's job; fluxing is limestone's.
The third trap is the iron(II)/iron(III) test swap. Fe²⁺ uses hexacyanoferrate(III); Fe³⁺ uses hexacyanoferrate(II). The reagents cross — answering the same reagent for both fails both items.
The fourth trap is wrought versus cast iron. Wrought is nearly pure and tough; cast is hard and brittle. Toughness belongs to the purer form, not the harder one.
A final trap is the direction of steelmaking. Oxygen removes carbon from pig iron to make steel; it never adds carbon. Any option describing carbon addition in a converter reverses the process.
bullets: CO reduces; coke burns; limestone fluxes.
Fe²⁺ → hexacyanoferrate(III); Fe³⁺ → hexacyanoferrate(II).
Wrought iron is tough; cast iron is brittle.
Crossed reagents, crossed reputations.

lessons.title: Copper and Alloys
lessons.objective: Identify the appropriate method of extraction of copper from its compounds, relate the properties of copper and its compounds to their uses, specify the method for the preparation of CuSO₄, specify the constituents and uses of alloys, and compare the properties and uses of alloys to pure metals.

content.heading: Copper and Alloys
paragraphs: The wire in a wall socket carries current because one metal conducts it better than almost any other. This lesson follows that metal from its rock to its alloys.

content.heading: Extracting copper
paragraphs: Copper is extracted from chalcopyrite (CuFeS₂) and other sulfide ores because it sits low in the reactivity series. The ore is concentrated by froth flotation, then roasted to copper(I) oxide, and reduced with carbon or by self-reduction to blister copper.

Blister copper is then purified by electrorefining: impure anodes dissolve, pure cathodes collect the metal. The process mirrors copper purification from the electrolysis lesson, with anode sludge recovering gold and silver.
Oxide ores follow a simpler route: carbon reduction directly, because copper is low enough for carbon to displace it. The series decides, as always.
bullets: Sulfide ores: concentrate, roast, self-reduce to blister copper.
Electrorefining purifies blister copper.
Carbon works because copper sits low in the series.
content.takeaway: Copper comes from sulfide ores by reduction, then electrorefining.

check.question: Blister copper is purified by
check.why: Electrorefining dissolves impure anodes and deposits pure copper on the cathode.

content.heading: Properties, uses and copper(II) sulfate
paragraphs: Copper is reddish-brown, soft, malleable, and the best common conductor of electricity after silver. Those properties explain its uses: electrical wiring, motors, coins and alloys. It does not rust like iron, though it tarnishes green in air.
Copper(II) tetraoxosulfate(VI) (CuSO₄) is prepared by reacting copper(II) oxide or carbonate with dilute sulfuric acid: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. The blue solution crystallises to blue pentahydrate.
The test for Cu²⁺ is ammonia solution, which first gives a pale blue precipitate of Cu(OH)₂ that dissolves in excess ammonia to a deep blue complex. That deep blue is specific to copper.
bullets: Reddish-brown, soft, best common conductor.
CuSO₄ from CuO + dilute H₂SO₄.
Cu²⁺ test: pale blue precipitate, deep blue in excess NH₃.
content.takeaway: Copper conducts best among common metals, and its blue test is unmistakable.

check.question: The test for Cu²⁺ with excess ammonia solution gives
check.why: Excess ammonia complexes copper(II) to the deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺.

content.heading: Alloys: mixtures with a purpose
paragraphs: An alloy is a mixture of metals (sometimes with non-metals) designed to beat the pure metal at some job. Steel is iron with carbon; stainless steel adds chromium and nickel. Brass is copper with zinc; bronze is copper with tin.

Duralumin is aluminium with copper and magnesium for aircraft. Type-metal is lead with antimony and tin for printing. Soft solder is lead with tin for joining. Permalloy (iron with nickel) and alnico (iron with aluminium, nickel and cobalt) serve in magnets.

Alloys are harder and stronger than the pure metals because foreign atoms break up the sliding planes of the electron sea. They resist rust better and melt lower. Pure metals are never the best choice when an alloy exists.
bullets: Steel = iron + C; stainless = + Cr, Ni.
Brass = Cu + Zn; bronze = Cu + Sn; duralumin = Al + Cu.
Alloys are harder, stronger and more rust-resistant.
content.takeaway: Alloys trade purity for hardness, strength and rust resistance.

check.question: Bronze is an alloy of
check.why: Bronze is copper alloyed with tin; brass is copper with zinc.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For alloy questions, name the two main metals first. Brass-zinc, bronze-tin, steel-iron: the pair is the answer's skeleton.

content.problem: Copper(II) sulfate is prepared from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. Write the equation and state the colour change.

steps.reason: A base (oxide) plus an acid gives a salt plus water
Black oxide dissolves to a blue solution
steps.result: Black CuO becomes blue CuSO₄ solution

steps.reason: The sulfate ion names it tetraoxosulfate(VI)

content.question: Why is copper preferred to aluminium for household wiring despite aluminium being lighter?
hints: Safety and losses decide household wiring

content.heading: Go deeper: Why copper wins wires
paragraphs: Silver conducts best, but price rules it out. Copper is second-best and far cheaper, which is why it owns household wiring. Aluminium conducts well per kilogram and wins overhead transmission lines, where weight matters more than volume.
The choice is therefore economic physics: conductivity per cost for wires, conductivity per weight for cables. The same metal ranking produces different winners in different jobs.
Copper's ductility also matters: it draws into thin wire without breaking. A conductor must be both conducting and drawable, and copper is the best compromise of the two.
A candidate who ranks by job rather than by metal will answer use questions correctly even for unfamiliar alloys.
Corrosion decides the rest: copper resists rusting far better than iron, which is why it survives in damp walls for decades. Conductivity, ductility and durability together close the case.
A candidate who needs a wiring answer should rank by the job (household, overhead, marine) before naming the metal. The job is the question; the metal is the conclusion.
bullets: Silver best but dear; copper second and affordable.
Aluminium wins overhead lines (per kilogram).
Ductility plus conductivity decides wiring.
Rank by job: cost, weight or drawable.

content.heading: Go deeper: Alloys and the electron sea
paragraphs: Pure metals are soft because their atoms slide past each other in the electron sea. Foreign atoms in an alloy pin those slides: the planes cannot move as freely, so the alloy is harder and stronger than either parent metal.
That is why steel beats iron, brass beats zinc, and bronze beats copper at their jobs. The alloying atoms are a deliberate obstruction, not an impurity.
Alloys also resist corrosion better: stainless steel's chromium film, brass's copper-rich surface, and bronze's patina all seal the metal from attack. Hardness and protection arrive together.
The exam contrast is purity versus purpose: pure metals are never the best choice when an alloy exists for the same job.
The same pinning explains why pure copper is too soft for coins and why bronze was chosen for bells: hardness is not a virtue in itself, only a fit for the job.
A candidate who sees every alloy as pinned pure metal will predict relative hardness from composition alone.
bullets: Foreign atoms pin the sliding planes — alloys are harder.
Steel, brass, bronze all beat their parents.
Alloy surfaces resist corrosion better.
Purpose beats purity in every alloy question.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in copper and alloys
paragraphs: The classic trap is the extraction route. Sulfide ores go through roasting and self-reduction; oxide ores go through carbon reduction. Naming carbon reduction for a sulfide ore reverses the method.
The second trap is the Cu²⁺ test direction. Pale blue precipitate first, deep blue solution in excess — reversing the order describes the wrong observation.
The third trap is brass versus bronze. Brass is copper with zinc; bronze is copper with tin. The two names are the most swapped pair in the syllabus.

The fourth trap is assuming pure metals are best. Every named alloy exists because it beats the pure metal at hardness, rust resistance or melting point — the comparison question always favours the alloy.
A final trap is the purity of blister copper. Blister copper is crude and electrorefining alone makes it pure; any option claiming the reduction step gives pure copper reverses the factory order.
A candidate who writes the two alloy pairs before reading the options eliminates half the distractors instantly.
bullets: Sulfides: roast + self-reduce. Oxides: carbon reduction.
Cu²⁺: pale blue first, deep blue in excess NH₃.
Brass = Cu + Zn; bronze = Cu + Sn.
Alloys always beat pure metals at their job.

lessons.title: Introduction to Organic Chemistry
lessons.objective: Derive the name of organic compounds from their general formulae, relate the name of a compound to its structure, relate the tetravalency of carbon to its ability to form chains of compound (catenation), classify compounds according to their functional groups, and derive empirical formula and molecular formula from given data.

content.heading: Introduction to Organic Chemistry
paragraphs: Soap, fuel, plastics and drugs are all built from one element's endless chains. This lesson explains why carbon — and only carbon — can build those chains, and how names are read from them.

content.heading: Why carbon forms chains
paragraphs: Carbon has four outer electrons, so it forms four bonds: it is tetravalent. Each bond can link to another carbon, so chains, rings and branches grow without limit. That ability to link carbon to carbon is called catenation.

No other element does this as well: silicon forms chains poorly, while nitrogen and oxygen stop at two or three bonds. Carbon's four bonds plus its strong carbon–carbon links make it the chain-builder of nature.

Inside every organic molecule the carbon skeleton carries functional groups — OH, COOH, NH₂ — small teams of atoms that decide the compound's behaviour. The skeleton gives the name's length; the group gives its personality.
bullets: Carbon is tetravalent: four bonds per atom.
Catenation = carbon linking to carbon in chains and rings.
Functional groups (OH, COOH, NH₂) decide behaviour.
content.takeaway: Carbon's four bonds let it chain without limit, and functional groups decide behaviour.

check.question: Catenation is the ability of carbon to
check.why: Catenation is carbon linking to carbon in chains, rings and branches.

content.heading: General formulae and naming
paragraphs: Each family of organic compounds has a general formula: alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, alkanols CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH. The n tells how many carbons; the formula then gives the hydrogens. Methane is C₁H₄, ethane C₂H₆.

The name reads the chain length and the group: 'eth' means two carbons, 'an' means single bonds, 'ene' means a double bond, 'yne' a triple bond, 'ol' an OH group, 'oic acid' a COOH group. Butane is four carbons, single bonds; ethene is two carbons with a double bond.
IUPAC names therefore encode structure: given the name, the skeleton can be drawn; given the skeleton, the name can be built. The skill is translation in both directions.
Isomer counting follows chain length: pentane (C5H12) has 3 structural isomers and hexane (C6H14) has 5, each drawn by rearranging the skeleton.
bullets: Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; alkenes CₙH₂ₙ; alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.
Name = chain length + bond type + functional group.
IUPAC names encode the skeleton both ways.
Isomers: C5H12 3 (n, iso, neo), C6H14 5.
content.takeaway: General formulae count hydrogens; names encode length, bonds and groups.

check.question: The general formula of the alkenes is
check.why: Alkenes have one double bond, so they carry two fewer hydrogens than alkanes.

content.heading: Empirical and molecular formulae
paragraphs: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula is the true count in one molecule. Glucose and fructose share the empirical formula CH₂O, but glucose is truly C₆H₁₂O₆.

Percentage composition gives the ratio: divide each percentage by its relative atomic mass, then by the smallest value. A compound of 92.3% carbon and 7.7% hydrogen gives 7.69 and 7.7, which reduce to CH — an empirical formula of CH.

The molecular formula follows from the molar mass: if the compound's Mr is 78 and CH weighs 13, then 78 ÷ 13 = 6, so the true formula is C₆H₆. Percentages alone never give the true formula — the molar mass scales the ratio up.
bullets: Empirical = simplest ratio; molecular = true count.
Divide percentages by Ar, then by the smallest.
Scale the ratio by Mr ÷ empirical Mr.
content.takeaway: Percentages give the ratio; the molar mass scales it to the true formula.

check.question: A compound has Mr = 78 and empirical formula CH. Its molecular formula is
check.why: CH weighs 13; 78 ÷ 13 = 6, so the formula is C₆H₆.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For any organic name, split it into length, bonds and group first. The three parts answer most naming questions before any chemistry is needed.

content.problem: A compound is 92.3% carbon and 7.7% hydrogen, with Mr = 78. Determine its molecular formula.

steps.reason: Carbon 92.3 ÷ 12, hydrogen 7.7 ÷ 1
The ratio must be whole numbers
CH weighs 13; the true Mr is 78

content.question: A compound is 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen. Give its empirical formula.
hints: Divide each percentage by its Ar (12, 1, 16)
Divide through by the smallest value

content.heading: Go deeper: Why carbon chains are endless
paragraphs: Carbon's four bonds and its strong carbon–carbon links let it form chains, rings and branches of any length. Silicon, directly below carbon, forms chains poorly because silicon–silicon bonds are weak; nitrogen and oxygen stop at two or three bonds.

That chain-building is catenation, and it is the reason organic chemistry exists as a subject: millions of compounds from one element's linking habit. Inorganic chemistry, by contrast, counts thousands.

The skeleton is not the whole story: functional groups hang off it and decide reactivity. The same chain length with an OH is an alkanol; with a COOH it is an acid. Skeleton plus group is the complete description.
A candidate who separates skeleton from group can classify any organic compound by naming its two parts.
The chain can also close into a ring, as in benzene, where six carbons form a loop. Rings are catenation too — the same linking habit bent into a circle.
A candidate who sees chains and rings as one habit will never treat benzene as a different kind of chemistry. It is the same carbon, looped.
bullets: Carbon chains uniquely well; silicon poorly, others not at all.
Millions of compounds from one linking habit.
Skeleton gives length; functional group gives behaviour.
Classify by skeleton + group, always.

content.heading: Go deeper: Homologous series and general formulae
paragraphs: A homologous series is a family differing by CH₂ units with the same functional group: methanol, ethanol, propanol. The fixed difference means properties change gradually down the series — boiling points rise, solubility falls — in a regular pattern.
The general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ for alkanes is that pattern in algebra: each extra carbon adds CH₂. Deriving a formula is therefore counting the difference, not memorising each member.
Gradual property change within a series is why the series concept matters: it predicts unseen members. A candidate who knows the pattern can state the properties of a compound never taught.
The exam loves that prediction: given the properties of two members, the third follows the trend. The series is a prophecy machine.
The regular property change is why the series concept matters beyond naming: it predicts the properties of unseen members, which is exactly what examination items test.
That prediction skill is also practical: a chemist who knows a series can estimate the boiling point of a compound nobody has measured yet.
bullets: Homologous series differ by CH₂ with one functional group.
Properties change gradually down a series.
General formulae are patterns, not lists.
Series predict unseen members’ properties.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in organic introduction
paragraphs: The classic trap is the empirical–molecular confusion. Percentages give the ratio only; without a molar mass the true formula cannot be known. Any option scaling the ratio without an Mr is wrong.

The second trap is the name–structure direction. 'Butene' names a four-carbon chain with a double bond; the double bond's position needs the number. Candidates who draw only the skeleton miss the position.
The third trap is tetravalency. Carbon forms four bonds always; structures with five bonds or with carbon carrying a charge in simple molecules violate the rule. Counting bonds is the check.

The fourth trap is treating functional groups as decoration. The -OH of an alkanol and the -OH of an acid behave differently because the group is embedded differently. The group decides, the skeleton merely carries.
A final trap is the abbreviation habit. Writing CH₃CH₂OH without recognising ethanol wastes the naming skill the question is testing. Expand structures before naming them.
bullets: Percentages give ratios; Mr gives true formulae.
Names encode chain, bonds and group together.
Carbon always forms four bonds.
Functional groups decide behaviour, not the skeleton.

lessons.title: Alkanes and Petroleum
lessons.objective: Relate the homologous series of alkanes to their physical properties, state the substitution reaction and a few examples and uses of halogenated products, derive structural isomers (not beyond six carbon atoms), identify crude oil as a complex mixture of hydrocarbons, relate the fractions to their properties and uses, relate transformation processes to quality improvement of the fractions, and state the quality of petrol and the meaning of octane number.

content.heading: Alkanes and Petroleum
paragraphs: From cooking gas to aviation fuel, one family of compounds powers daily life. This lesson follows them from crude oil to the petrol in a tank.

content.heading: Alkanes: the saturated family
paragraphs: Alkanes are hydrocarbons with only single bonds: general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (methane, ethane, propane, butane...). They are saturated, meaning every carbon holds the maximum hydrogens, and they are the petroleum family.

Physical properties change gradually down the series: melting and boiling points rise with chain length, and density increases. Methane is a gas at room temperature; hexane is a liquid; waxes are solids. The pattern is the homologous series at work.

Alkanes react mainly by substitution: in ultraviolet light a hydrogen is replaced by a halogen. CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, then CH₃Cl + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + HCl. The reaction needs light, and products are mixtures.

Halogenated products were widely used: chloroform served as an anaesthetic, carbon tetrachloride as a solvent and in fire extinguishers, and DDT as an insecticide. DDT's persistence later led to its restriction.
bullets: Alkanes: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, single bonds only, saturated.
Boiling point rises with chain length.
Substitution: UV light replaces H with halogen.
Uses: chloroform anaesthetic, CCl4 solvent/fire extinguishing, DDT insecticide.
content.takeaway: Alkanes are saturated chains whose properties climb with length.

check.question: The substitution reaction of alkanes needs
check.why: UV light provides the energy to replace hydrogen with halogen.

content.heading: Isomerism in plain words
paragraphs: Isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures — same atoms, different arrangements. Butane has two structures: the straight chain and the branched chain (methylpropane). Both are C₄H₁₀.
Structural isomerism rearranges the carbon skeleton: n-butane and isobutane. The exam limits examples to six carbon atoms, which is plenty to show the idea.
Isomers have different properties because arrangement decides shape. The branched isomer boils lower than the straight chain, which is why refining adjusts isomer ratios.
The branched isomer is more compact, so its molecules attract each other less strongly and it boils lower. Arrangement changes the contact between molecules, and contact decides boiling.
bullets: Isomers: same formula, different arrangement.
C₄H₁₀: n-butane and methylpropane.
Arrangement changes boiling point and properties.
Compact isomers attract less and boil lower.
content.takeaway: Same atoms, different skeletons, different properties.

check.question: n-Butane and methylpropane are
check.why: Both are C₄H₁₀ with different carbon arrangements — structural isomers.

content.heading: Petroleum: from crude oil to fractions
paragraphs: Crude oil is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons, mostly alkanes, formed from ancient organisms. It is separated by fractional distillation: heated to vapour, then cooled in a tower where fractions condense at their boiling points.

The tower gives, from bottom to top: bitumen, fuel oil, kerosene, petrol (gasoline), petroleum gas. Each fraction has its own boiling range and its own use — petrol for cars, kerosene for jets, bitumen for roads.

Cracking and reforming improve the fractions: cracking breaks long chains into shorter, more valuable ones, and reforming reshapes them into better fuels. Petrochemicals are the starting materials of organic syntheses — plastics, drugs and detergents all begin here.
Feedstocks from refining and cracking are ethene, propene, benzene, toluene and xylene, ready for polymer and solvent manufacture.
bullets: Crude oil = complex mixture of hydrocarbons.
Fractional distillation gives petrol to bitumen.
Cracking shortens chains; reforming improves quality.
Petrochemicals feed plastics, drugs and detergents.
Feedstocks: ethene, propene, benzene, toluene, xylene.
content.takeaway: Fractional distillation sorts crude oil by boiling point into useful fractions.

check.question: Petroleum is separated into fractions by
check.why: Fractions condense at different boiling points in the fractionating tower.

visual.caption: Heating turns crude oil to vapour, then cooling in the tower separates fractions by boiling point.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Octane number measures petrol quality: higher means less knocking in the engine. The number is a performance rating, not a composition.

content.problem: Butane (C₄H₁₀) burns completely: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O. Calculate the volume of oxygen at s.t.p. needed to burn 5.8 g of butane. (Ar C = 12, H = 1)

steps.reason: Moles = mass ÷ Mr

steps.operation: Apply the equation ratio and gas volume
steps.reason: 2 mol butane needs 13 mol O₂, so 0.10 mol needs 0.65 mol; 1 mol = 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.

content.question: 2.9 g of butane burns completely. Calculate the oxygen volume at s.t.p. (Mr = 58).
hints: Oxygen needed is 13/2 times the butane moles

content.heading: Go deeper: Substitution and why products are mixtures
paragraphs: Substitution replaces one hydrogen at a time, so chlorination of methane gives CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄ together. Separating them is fractional distillation; the product mix is a direct consequence of successive substitution.
Ultraviolet light starts the process by breaking chlorine molecules into atoms, which then pull hydrogens off the alkane. The light is the initiator, not a reagent.
Because every hydrogen is replaceable, halogenated alkanes are made as mixtures and separated by boiling point. The chemistry is simple; the engineering is the separation.
A candidate who writes successive substitution equations will never call a single product 'the' product of chlorination.

The successive products also differ in reactivity, so controlling the chlorine supply controls the distribution. Less chlorine favours mono-substitution; excess favours the fully substituted carbon tetrachloride.
That control is an industrial lever: the product mix is chosen by the chlorine dose, not by luck.
bullets: Substitution gives CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄ together.
UV light initiates by splitting Cl₂ into atoms.
Products are separated by fractional distillation.
No single product — a boiling-point ladder.

content.heading: Go deeper: Octane number and petrol quality
paragraphs: Octane number rates a petrol's resistance to knocking — the rattling when fuel ignites too early in the cylinder. The scale runs from isooctane (100) to n-heptane (0), and a petrol's number is the isooctane percentage of a reference mixture that knocks the same.
Higher octane fuel allows higher compression ratios, so engines run more efficiently. That is why premium petrol costs more: the octane number is bought, not given.
Branched-chain hydrocarbons have higher octane numbers than straight chains, which is why reforming and isomerisation raise petrol quality. Molecular shape, not just length, decides performance.
The exam trap is to treat octane number as composition. It is a performance rating — two petrols with the same octane number can have different compositions.
Blending is the third lever: a low-octane fraction blended with a high-octane one reaches a target number. Petrol quality is therefore a mixture calculation as much as a refining one.
A candidate who sees blending as averaging octane numbers will predict the result of any blend question.
Lead once raised octane cheaply, but its toxicity ended the practice. Modern high-octane petrol is blended from reformate and oxygenates instead — quality without poison.
A candidate who links the octane scale to blending and reforming answers quality questions that name no specific additive.
bullets: Octane number = resistance to knocking (isooctane = 100).
Higher octane allows higher compression, better efficiency.
Branched chains knock less than straight chains.
Octane number is a rating, not a composition.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in alkanes and petroleum
paragraphs: The classic trap is the general formula. Alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — the saturated family. Alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ) and alkynes (CₙH₂ₙ₋₂) differ by two hydrogens per bond. Counting the bonds gives the formula, not the other way round.

The second trap is isomer counting. Structural isomers rearrange the skeleton; geometric isomers (cis/trans) rearrange around a double bond. The two types belong to different families and are never interchangeable.
The third trap is the fractionating tower order. Petrol comes off near the top, bitumen at the bottom. Reversing them reverses every fraction's boiling point.
The fourth trap is cracking's purpose. Cracking shortens chains to meet demand for petrol; it does not purify crude oil. Purification is distillation's job.
A final trap is the substitution mechanism. It is a free-radical chain, not an ionic one, so polar-solver arguments do not apply. Light initiates; radicals propagate; termination ends the chain.
bullets: Count the bonds to get the formula.
Structural rearranges skeletons; geometric around double bonds.
Petrol top, bitumen bottom in the tower.
Cracking shortens chains; distillation purifies.

lessons.title: Alkenes and Alkynes
lessons.objective: Distinguish structural and geometric isomerism, state additional and polymerization reactions, give polythene and synthetic rubber as products of polymerization and their use in vulcanization, and state the production of ethyne from calcium carbide with its simple reactions and properties, with chemical tests for alkenes and terminal alkynes.

content.heading: Alkenes and Alkynes
paragraphs: If alkanes are saturated chains, alkenes and alkynes are the same chains with one or two kinks of unsaturation. Those kinks make them reactive — and that reactivity is the whole lesson.

content.heading: Alkenes: one double bond
paragraphs: Alkenes have one carbon–carbon double bond: general formula CₙH₂ₙ (ethene C₂H₄, propene C₃H₆). The double bond is reactive: it opens up to add atoms across it. Bromine water is decolourised by alkenes — the orange colour disappears as bromine adds — and that is the alkene test.

Geometric isomerism (cis/trans) appears around the double bond because it cannot rotate. In cis-but-2-ene the two methyl groups sit on the same side; in trans-but-2-ene they sit opposite. Same formula, different geometry, different boiling points.
Alkenes polymerise: ethene joins into polythene (polyethylene), the plastic of bags and bottles. The double bond opens to link thousands of molecules into one long chain.
bullets: Alkenes: CₙH₂ₙ with one C=C double bond.
Test: bromine water decolourised (addition across the double bond).
Cis/trans isomerism around the double bond.
Ethene polymerises to polythene.
content.takeaway: The double bond adds, isomerises and polymerises — the alkene signature.

check.question: The test for an alkene is
check.why: Alkenes add bromine across the double bond, discharging its orange colour.

visual.caption: Alkenes add across the double bond, so bromine water is discharged, while saturated alkanes do not.

content.heading: Addition and polymerisation
paragraphs: Addition opens the double bond to add two atoms, one to each carbon. Ethene + H₂ → ethane (with nickel catalyst); ethene + Br₂ → dibromoethane; ethene + HCl → chloroethane. The double bond becomes a single bond.

Polymerisation is addition repeated thousands of times: ethene chains link into polythene. Synthetic rubber is made the same way from diene monomers, then vulcanised — heated with sulfur — to cross-link the chains and harden the rubber.
Addition and polymerisation are the same chemistry at two scales: opening double bonds. The products differ only in how many molecules join.
bullets: Addition: H₂, Br₂, HCl add across C=C.
Polymerisation: double bonds link into long chains.
Vulcanisation cross-links rubber with sulfur.
content.takeaway: Alkenes add and chain together through their double bond.

check.question: Polythene is made by the polymerisation of
check.why: Polythene is the polymer of ethene, linked through its double bond.

content.heading: Alkynes and ethyne
paragraphs: Alkynes have one carbon–carbon triple bond: general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (ethyne C₂H₂, propyne C₃H₄). The triple bond adds twice — ethyne adds two molecules of hydrogen, then two of bromine.
Ethyne is produced from calcium carbide and water: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂. It burns with a very hot flame (oxy-ethyne welding) because its combustion releases great energy.
Terminal alkynes (with H on the triple bond, like ethyne) give a red precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate — the specific test. Non-terminal alkynes do not.
bullets: Alkynes: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ with one C≡C triple bond.
Ethyne: CaC₂ + water; welding flame.
Terminal alkyne test: red precipitate with ammoniacal AgNO₃.
content.takeaway: Alkynes add twice across the triple bond; ethyne is the carbide product.

check.question: Ethyne is prepared from calcium carbide by reaction with
check.why: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂ gives ethyne.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For unsaturation questions, count the additions: alkene adds once, alkyne adds twice. The count of molecules added names the family.

content.problem: Ethene reacts with bromine. Write the equation and calculate the mass of dibromoethane formed from 2.8 g of ethene. (Ar C = 12, H = 1, Br = 80)

steps.reason: Bromine adds across the double bond, one molecule per ethene
Mr(C₂H₄) = 28, so grams convert by dividing by 28
One mole of ethene gives one mole of product; Mr(C₂H₄Br₂) = 188

content.question: 5.6 g of ethene reacts with excess bromine. Calculate the mass of dibromoethane formed. (Mr ethene = 28, product = 188)

content.heading: Go deeper: Cis, trans and why geometry matters
paragraphs: A double bond cannot rotate, so groups fixed on its carbons stay in their positions. In cis-but-2-ene both methyl groups sit on the same side; in trans-but-2-ene they sit opposite. The two isomers have different boiling points and reactivity.
Geometric isomerism exists only where each double-bond carbon carries two different groups. But-2-ene shows it; ethene and propene cannot, because one carbon lacks two different groups.
The distinction matters because shape changes contact between molecules: cis isomers attract differently and boil differently. Geometry is a property, not just a drawing.
A candidate who checks the two groups on each carbon before declaring cis/trans will never invent geometric isomers where none exist.

That fixed geometry is also why cis and trans isomers can be separated by boiling point: the same-side arrangement packs differently and attracts differently. Geometry is a physical property, not just a drawing convention.
A candidate who checks the two groups on each carbon before declaring cis or trans will never invent geometric isomers where none can exist.

That fixed geometry is also why cis and trans isomers can be separated by boiling point: the same-side arrangement packs differently and attracts differently. Geometry is a physical property, not just a drawing convention.
bullets: Double bonds cannot rotate — geometry is fixed.
Cis: same side; trans: opposite side.
Needs two different groups on each carbon.
Geometry changes boiling point and reactivity.

content.heading: Go deeper: Polymers and vulcanisation
paragraphs: Addition polymerisation links monomers through their double bonds into long chains: ethene to polythene, styrene to polystyrene. The polymer's properties come from chain length and cross-linking, not from new chemistry.

Natural rubber is too soft and sticky for tyres. Vulcanisation heats it with sulfur, which forms cross-links between chains and makes it hard, elastic and durable. Every tyre on the road is vulcanised rubber.

Condensation polymerisation is the other route: monomers join with small molecules lost, as in nylon and terylene. Addition versus condensation is decided by whether a small molecule appears in the equation.
The exam chain is therefore: double bond → addition → polymer → cross-linking. Each step explains the next product's properties.
The same addition chemistry also explains why polythene is thermoplastic: its chains are separate and slide on heating. Vulcanised rubber, by contrast, is cross-linked and cannot flow.
A candidate who separates chain-making from cross-linking keeps two processes distinct in every polymer answer.
bullets: Addition polymerisation: monomers link through double bonds.
Vulcanisation cross-links rubber with sulfur.
Condensation loses small molecules (nylon, terylene).
Properties come from chain length and cross-linking.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in unsaturation
paragraphs: The classic trap is the carbonyl test. Bromine water is decolourised by alkenes (addition) but not by alkanes. Any option claiming alkanes decolourise bromine water is false.

The second trap is the terminal alkyne test. Only alkynes with hydrogen on the triple bond give the red precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate. Internal alkynes fail the test — terminal is the condition.
The third trap is polymerisation versus addition. Both use double bonds; polymerisation repeats the addition thousands of times. Naming the scale decides the answer.
The fourth trap is geometric isomerism in molecules without two different groups on each carbon. But-2-ene has it; ethene does not. The groups must be checked first.
A final trap is ethyne addition count. Ethyne adds two molecules of hydrogen or bromine across the triple bond, not one. The count of molecules added names the family.
bullets: Alkenes decolourise bromine water; alkanes do not.
Only terminal alkynes give the red AgNO₃ precipitate.
Polymerisation is addition repeated thousands of times.
Geometric isomerism needs two different groups per carbon.

lessons.title: Benzene
lessons.objective: Relate the properties of benzene to its structure, distinguish aliphatic from aromatic hydrocarbons, and state the structure, properties and uses of benzene.

content.heading: Benzene
paragraphs: Some hydrocarbons are rings, not chains — and the most important ring is a sweet-smelling liquid called benzene. This lesson explains its structure and why it behaves so differently from its chain cousins.

content.heading: A ring of six carbons
paragraphs: Benzene (C₆H₆) has six carbon atoms arranged in a ring, each carrying one hydrogen. The ring is not three double bonds and three single bonds — the electrons are shared around the whole ring, which is called delocalisation.

That delocalisation makes benzene more stable than a simple ring with alternating double bonds would be. It needs more energy to break than expected, which is why benzene resists the easy addition reactions of alkenes.
Because of its structure, benzene is aromatic — a sweet smell and a ring of shared electrons — while alkanes and alkenes are aliphatic. Aromatic means ring-based, not just 'smelling nice'.
bullets: Benzene: C₆H₆, a six-carbon ring with delocalised electrons.
Delocalisation makes it more stable than expected.
Aromatic = ring-based; aliphatic = chain-based.
content.takeaway: Benzene is a delocalised six-carbon ring — aromatic, not aliphatic.

check.question: Benzene is classified as aromatic because
options: It contains a ring of delocalised electrons
It is a liquid at room temperature
It burns with a sooty flame
check.why: Aromatic means a ring of shared (delocalised) electrons, not a smell.

content.heading: How benzene reacts
paragraphs: Benzene burns like other hydrocarbons: C₆H₆ + 7½O₂ → 6CO₂ + 3H₂O. But it resists addition: bromine water is not decolourised in the dark, unlike alkenes. With iron(III) chloride and bromine, it undergoes substitution instead — a hydrogen is replaced by bromine.
That resistance to addition is the delocalisation at work. The ring protects its shared electrons, so benzene prefers substitution (swapping H) over addition (breaking the ring's bonds).

Benzene is prepared industrially from coal tar and by reforming petroleum. Its uses include making plastics, detergents, dyes, pharmaceuticals and solvents — it is a starting material, not just a fuel.
bullets: Burns completely: C₆H₆ + 7½O₂ → 6CO₂ + 3H₂O.
Resists addition; undergoes substitution (with FeCl₃/Br₂).
From coal tar or petroleum reforming.
Uses: plastics, detergents, dyes, drugs, solvents.
content.takeaway: Benzene substitutes instead of adding — its ring protects its electrons.

check.question: Bromine water is not decolourised by benzene in the dark because
options: Bromine does not react with rings
check.why: Delocalisation stabilises the ring, so benzene undergoes substitution, not addition.

content.heading: Structure explains behaviour
paragraphs: The delocalised ring has equal bond lengths between all carbons — neither single nor double, but in between. That equality is measurable and proves the sharing is real, not a drawing convention.
Substitution preserves the ring: a hydrogen is swapped out and the delocalised system survives. Addition would break the ring and lose the stability, so it does not happen under normal conditions.
That is why benzene's properties cannot be predicted from ethene's. The ring is a different kind of unsaturation — shared, not localised — and its chemistry follows the sharing.
bullets: All C–C bonds in benzene are equal (delocalised).
Substitution preserves the ring; addition would break it.
Ring unsaturation ≠ double-bond unsaturation.
content.takeaway: Delocalisation makes benzene substitute where alkenes add.

check.question: In benzene, all carbon–carbon bonds are
check.why: The electrons are shared around the ring, equalising all bond lengths.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For any benzene item, ask first whether the reagent adds or substitutes. Benzene substitutes — the ring survives — and that one word decides the answer.

content.problem: Benzene burns completely: C₆H₆ + 7½O₂ → 6CO₂ + 3H₂O. Calculate the volume of oxygen at s.t.p. needed to burn 7.8 g of benzene. (Mr benzene = 78)

steps.reason: One mole of benzene needs 7.5 moles of oxygen
One mole of gas fills 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.

content.question: 15.6 g of benzene burns completely. Calculate the oxygen volume at s.t.p. (Mr = 78).
hints: Oxygen needed is 7.5 times the benzene moles

content.heading: Go deeper: Delocalisation made visible
paragraphs: X-ray measurements show all six C–C bonds in benzene are equal at 139 pm — between single (154 pm) and double (134 pm) lengths. The structure is a perfect hexagon, not a triangle of alternating bonds.
That equality is the direct evidence for delocalisation: if three double bonds existed, the molecule would show two bond lengths. It shows one.
The extra stability from delocalisation is called resonance energy, and it is why benzene needs more energy to hydrogenate than three isolated double bonds would suggest.
A candidate who links the bond-length evidence to the substitution behaviour has explained benzene completely — structure, proof and chemistry in one chain.
The stability that follows is measurable as heat: hydrogenating benzene releases less energy than three separate double bonds would, and the difference is the resonance energy.
That energy gap is why benzene resists addition: breaking the ring would pay the resonance energy as a penalty.
A candidate who can state the gap has explained both the structure and the chemistry from one number.
bullets: All C–C bonds equal at 139 pm — direct evidence.
Delocalisation gives resonance energy.
Equal bonds prove sharing; alternating bonds would not.
One chain: structure → evidence → behaviour.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why substitution preserves the ring
paragraphs: Substitution swaps one hydrogen for a substituent while the delocalised system reforms. The ring's stability is temporarily lost during the attack but restored when the hydrogen leaves — the net result keeps the aromatic sextet intact.
Addition, by contrast, would saturate two carbons and break the ring's shared system permanently. Benzene 'chooses' substitution because substitution is the only path that keeps the stability.
That is why bromination needs iron(III) chloride: the catalyst generates the electrophile that attacks the ring, and the ring's response is substitution, not addition.
The exam logic is therefore thermodynamic: benzene does what keeps it aromatic. Any option breaking the ring contradicts the stability.
The intermediate in substitution is temporarily non-aromatic, which is why the reaction needs a catalyst and still proceeds: the stability of the ring is recovered in the final step.
That temporary loss also explains why benzene substitutes more slowly than alkenes react. Stability slows everything it touches.
bullets: Substitution keeps the aromatic sextet; addition breaks it.
FeCl₃ generates the electrophile for bromination.
The ring chooses the path that preserves stability.
Breaking the ring is never the favoured route.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in benzene
paragraphs: The classic trap is the formula. Benzene is C₆H₆ — three degrees of unsaturation by ring plus double bonds — and candidates who write C₆H₁₂ name a saturated ring that cannot exist in the syllabus.

The second trap is addition versus substitution. Bromine water is not decolourised in the dark; bromination needs FeCl₃ and proceeds by substitution. Conflating the two conditions reverses both answers.
The third trap is 'aromatic' meaning 'smelling nice'. The syllabus meaning is structural: a ring of delocalised electrons. Smell never decides classification.
The fourth trap is structure drawings. Alternating double bonds are a convention; the true structure has equal bonds. Options describing three separate double bonds misstate the delocalisation.
A final trap is equating aromatic with aliphatic. Aliphatic hydrocarbons are open chains; aromatic ones are rings. Benzene is aromatic, and every paragraph of its chemistry starts from that ring.
A candidate who classifies first and reacts second will never apply alkene logic to a ring compound.
A candidate who writes the delocalised structure before answering any benzene item has already avoided most of these traps.
bullets: Benzene is C₆H₆ — unsaturation from ring + bonds.
No decolourisation in the dark; FeCl₃ gives substitution.
Aromatic is structural, not a smell.
Equal bonds: delocalisation is real, not a drawing.

lessons.title: Alkanols
lessons.objective: Compare the various classes of alkanols, determine the processes involved in ethanol production, examine the importance of ethanol as an alternative energy provider, distinguish the various classes of alkanols, give local examples of fermentation and distillation (gin from palm wine), explain glycerol as a polyhydric alkanol, and state the oxidation test distinguishing primary, secondary and tertiary alkanols (Lucas test).

content.heading: Alkanols
paragraphs: Drinking spirits, hand sanitiser and fuel all share one family: the alkanols, alcohols with an –OH group. This lesson follows ethanol from palm wine to petrol tank, and the test that tells the alcohol classes apart.

content.heading: Primary, secondary and tertiary
paragraphs: Alkanols carry the hydroxyl group (–OH) on carbon. The class depends on how many other carbons share that carbon: primary (1°) alcohols have the OH on a carbon bonded to one other carbon (ethanol); secondary (2°) on two (propan-2-ol); tertiary (3°) on three (2-methylpropan-2-ol).

That single difference decides reactivity: primary alkanols oxidise to aldehydes then acids; secondary oxidise to ketones; tertiary resist oxidation altogether. The more carbons around the OH, the less the OH can be attacked.
The classes also differ in boiling point and solubility, both falling as the chain branches. Structure at the OH carbon is the whole story.
bullets: OH on 1 carbon = primary; 2 = secondary; 3 = tertiary.
Primary oxidises to aldehyde then acid; secondary to ketone; tertiary resists.
Branching lowers boiling point and solubility.
content.takeaway: Count the carbons on the OH carbon to name the class.

check.question: Propan-2-ol is a secondary alkanol because its OH carbon is bonded to
check.why: A secondary alcohol has its OH on a carbon bonded to two other carbons.

content.heading: Ethanol by fermentation and distillation
paragraphs: Fermentation is yeast converting sugar to ethanol: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Palm wine ferments this way — wild yeast turns the sap sugary to alcoholic within days. The CO₂ bubbles are the fermentation visible.

Distillation then concentrates the ethanol: palm wine is distilled to gin, raising the alcohol from a few percent to drinking strength. The same fermentation-plus-distillation makes ethanol from cassava, maize and sugar cane worldwide.
Ethanol from petroleum is made by hydrating ethene. Both routes give the same molecule; the source decides cost, not the product.
bullets: Fermentation: yeast, sugar → ethanol + CO₂.
Palm wine → gin by distillation.
Petroleum route: hydration of ethene.
content.takeaway: Yeast ferments sugar to ethanol; distillation concentrates it.

check.question: The fermentation of glucose to ethanol also produces
check.why: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ — carbon(IV) oxide bubbles off.

content.heading: The Lucas test and glycerol
paragraphs: The Lucas test distinguishes the three classes: concentrated HCl with ZnCl₂ (Lucas reagent) replaces OH with Cl at rates that differ by class. Tertiary alcohols react instantly, secondary within minutes, primary only on heating. The cloudiness appearing is the reaction.
Oxidation also distinguishes them: primary gives aldehyde then acid, secondary gives ketone, tertiary gives no reaction. Two independent tests agree, which is why both are asked.
Glycerol is a trihydric alkanol — three OH groups on one molecule. It is syrupy, sweet, and used in soap, lotions and explosives (nitroglycerine). It is the polyhydric example the syllabus asks for.
bullets: Lucas reagent: tertiary instant, secondary minutes, primary on heating.
Oxidation: 1° → aldehyde → acid; 2° → ketone; 3° → none.
Glycerol: three OH groups; soap, lotions, explosives.
content.takeaway: Lucas cloudiness and oxidation agree: class decides reactivity.

check.question: In the Lucas test, the fastest cloudiness comes from
check.why: Tertiary alcohols react with Lucas reagent almost instantly.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For class questions, count the carbons on the OH carbon first. The count (1, 2 or 3) names the class before any property is considered.

content.problem: Ethanol burns completely: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. Calculate the volume of oxygen at s.t.p. needed to burn 4.6 g of ethanol. (Mr ethanol = 46)

steps.reason: One mole of ethanol needs three moles of oxygen
One mole of gas fills 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.

content.question: 9.2 g of ethanol burns completely. Calculate the oxygen volume at s.t.p. (Mr = 46).
hints: Oxygen needed is 3 times the ethanol moles

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the classes react differently
paragraphs: Oxidation must remove hydrogen from the OH carbon. Primary alcohols have two hydrogens there, so they oxidise twice (aldehyde, then acid). Secondary have one, so they oxidise once to a ketone. Tertiary have none, so oxidation stops — there is no hydrogen to remove.

The Lucas order follows the same carbocation stability: tertiary carbocations form fastest, so tertiary alcohols react instantly. The substitution rate is the stability of the intermediate, read as a clock.
Both tests are therefore the same chemistry seen twice: the substitution detail of the OH carbon decides everything. Class is not a label; it is a mechanism count.
A candidate who counts hydrogens on the OH carbon predicts oxidation and Lucas behaviour without memorising either.
That is also why tertiary alcohols dehydrate fastest: the same stable carbocation that speeds substitution also speeds elimination. One intermediate explains three behaviours.
A candidate who names the carbocation has connected substitution, elimination and oxidation in one idea.
A candidate who counts hydrogens on the OH carbon predicts oxidation and Lucas behaviour without memorising either.
The same counting habit classifies many later families, so the skill outlives this lesson.
It also pays off in every later family.
bullets: Oxidation removes H from the OH carbon: 1° twice, 2° once, 3° never.
Lucas rate follows carbocation stability: 3° fastest.
Class is a mechanism count, not a label.
Count hydrogens on the OH carbon to predict both.

content.heading: Go deeper: Ethanol as an energy provider
paragraphs: Ethanol burns to CO₂ and water, releasing energy without the sulfur and lead pollutants of petrol. Blending it into petrol (gasohol) raises octane and reduces emissions, which is why many countries mandate blends.
The catch is the source: fermentation needs farm land and water, and distillation needs energy. Ethanol is renewable but not free — its energy cost must be paid at the distillery.
That balance explains both the promise and the limit: ethanol works as an alternative energy provider where feedstock is cheap, and struggles where land competes with food.
The exam link is therefore economic as much as chemical: ethanol's value is its cleanliness, its cost is its farming.
Second-generation ethanol from waste biomass aims to escape the food-versus-fuel conflict entirely. The chemistry is identical; only the feedstock changes.
The exam link is therefore direct: ethanol’s value is its cleanliness, and its cost is its farming.
bullets: Ethanol burns clean (CO₂ + H₂O) and raises octane.
Renewable but land- and energy-hungry.
Blend value: octane up, emissions down.
Cleanliness is the value; farming is the cost.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in alkanols
paragraphs: The classic trap is the class count. The OH carbon's neighbours decide: ethanol is primary (one neighbour), propan-2-ol secondary (two), 2-methylpropan-2-ol tertiary (three). Counting total carbons instead of neighbours misnames every case.
The second trap is oxidation products. Primary gives aldehyde then acid in two steps; secondary gives ketone and stops. Any option giving a ketone from a primary alcohol reverses the sequence.
The third trap is the Lucas direction. Tertiary is fastest, primary slowest — the order is the reverse of oxidation ease. Mixing the two orders is the favourite error.
The fourth trap is glycerol's class. Three OH groups make it trihydric, not tertiary. Hydric counts OH groups; primary/secondary/tertiary counts neighbours. The two words are not interchangeable.
A final trap is fermentation direction. Yeast converts sugar to ethanol, never the reverse. Any option making ethanol the starting material of fermentation reverses the process.
bullets: Count neighbours of the OH carbon, not total carbons.
Primary → aldehyde → acid; secondary → ketone.
Lucas order is reverse of oxidation ease.
Trihydric counts OH groups; tertiary counts neighbours.

lessons.title: Alkanals and Alkanones
lessons.objective: Differentiate between alkanals and alkanones, giving the chemical test to distinguish them.

content.heading: Alkanals and Alkanones
paragraphs: The next family after alcohols carries a double bond to oxygen — a carbonyl group. This lesson follows the two carbonyl families and the test that tells them apart.

content.heading: Aldehydes and ketones
paragraphs: Alkanals (aldehydes) carry the carbonyl group at the end of the chain: the carbon has a hydrogen attached. Ethanal is CH₃CHO. Ketones (alkanones) carry it in the middle: propanone is CH₃COCH₃. End versus middle is the whole distinction.

Aldehydes oxidise easily to carboxylic acids, because the aldehyde hydrogen can be removed. Ketones resist further oxidation — there is no hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon to remove. That one hydrogen decides the chemistry.
Both families are made by oxidising alcohols: primary alkanols give alkanals, secondary give alkanones. The oxidation ladder from the alkanols lesson continues here.
bullets: Aldehydes: carbonyl at the end, with a hydrogen (ethanal).
Ketones: carbonyl in the middle, no hydrogen (propanone).
Aldehydes oxidise to acids; ketones resist.
Made by oxidising primary and secondary alkanols respectively.
content.takeaway: Aldehydes end with a hydrogen; ketones bury the carbonyl in the middle.

check.question: Propanone is a ketone because
options: Its carbonyl carbon has no hydrogen
It burns with a blue flame
check.why: In propanone (CH₃COCH₃) the carbonyl carbon carries two methyl groups and no hydrogen.

content.heading: Tollens test and the silver mirror
paragraphs: Tollens' reagent is an ammoniacal silver nitrate solution used to warm aldehydes. Aldehydes reduce silver ions to metallic silver, which deposits as a shiny mirror on the tube walls. Ketones do not reduce it — no mirror forms.
Fehling's and Benedict's solutions give the same distinction: aldehydes reduce blue copper(II) to red copper(I) oxide, while ketones leave the blue unchanged. Two independent reagents agree.
The silver mirror is the classic laboratory result: a clean tube, warmed with an aldehyde, comes out silvered inside. It is the specific test for the aldehyde group.
bullets: Tollens: aldehydes give a silver mirror; ketones do not.
Fehling/Benedict: aldehydes give red Cu₂O; ketones do not.
The aldehyde hydrogen is the reducing agent.
content.takeaway: Aldehydes reduce Tollens and Fehling; ketones do neither.

check.question: A compound gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. It is
check.why: Only aldehydes reduce silver ions to metallic silver.

content.heading: Properties and uses
paragraphs: Aldehydes and ketones are polar, hydrogen-bonding liquids, soluble in water when small. Their boiling points rise with chain length, and both families are used as solvents and intermediates.
Formaldehyde (methanal) preserves specimens and makes plastics; acetone (propanone) is a nail-polish remover and industrial solvent. Flavouring aldehydes perfume foods and soaps.
The carbonyl group decides both families' chemistry: it is the site of addition reactions (hydrogen, HCN) and of the oxidation that separates them.
Their polarity also lets small members dissolve in water, which is why formaldehyde is sold as a solution and acetone mixes with water freely.
bullets: Polar, hydrogen-bonding, water-soluble when small.
Formaldehyde: preservative, plastics. Acetone: solvent.
Carbonyl group is the reactive site.
content.takeaway: Both families share the carbonyl group; only aldehydes can be oxidised further.

check.question: Acetone (propanone) is used as
check.why: Propanone is a common solvent, including in nail-polish remover.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For carbonyl questions, first ask whether the carbonyl carbon carries a hydrogen. If yes, aldehyde; if no, ketone — and the tests follow.

content.problem: Ethanal is oxidised to ethanoic acid. Write the oxidation and state the change in oxidation number of the carbonyl carbon.

steps.reason: Aldehydes oxidise to carboxylic acids

steps.operation: Find the carbonyl carbon's number in ethanal
steps.reason: CH₃ is −3 overall; the double bond to O adds +2, the H adds −1
COOH carbon loses the H and gains an OH oxygen

content.question: Propanone is warmed with Tollens' reagent. Predict the result and give the reason.
hints: No silver mirror forms — the solution stays unchanged

content.heading: Go deeper: Why aldehydes oxidise and ketones refuse
paragraphs: Oxidation removes the hydrogen from the carbonyl carbon. Aldehydes have one to remove, so they oxidise to acids. Ketones have none — both neighbours are carbons — so oxidation would need to break a carbon–carbon bond, which does not happen under these conditions.
