That is why the oxidation ladder stops at ketones in the alkanol series: primary gives aldehyde then acid, secondary gives ketone and stops, tertiary gives nothing. The carbonyl neighbourhood decides the fate.
The same neighbourhood explains Tollens' reagent: only the aldehyde hydrogen can reduce silver ions. A ketone offers no hydrogen, so no mirror forms.
One hydrogen atom thus decides two famous tests — a candidate who counts it predicts both.
The same count explains the boiling points and reactivity patterns of the two families. Reaction chemistry, in this topic, is hydrogen counting from start to finish.
A candidate who counts first and names second never confuses the families under time pressure.
bullets: Oxidation removes the carbonyl hydrogen.
Aldehydes have one; ketones have none.
Tollens and Fehling both exploit that hydrogen.
One atom decides both famous tests.

content.heading: Go deeper: Silver mirror and Fehling mechanisms
paragraphs: In Tollens' test, silver ions are complexed by ammonia into [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺. The aldehyde reduces them to metallic silver, which nucleates on the glass as a mirror. The aldehyde itself is oxidised to a carboxylate.
In Fehling's test, blue copper(II) is reduced by the aldehyde to red copper(I) oxide. The colour change blue → red is the visible oxidation.
Both reagents are oxidising agents with a colour signal: silver mirror for one, red precipitate for the other. Ketones fail both because they cannot be oxidised under these conditions.
A candidate who writes the aldehyde as the reductant in both equations connects the two tests mechanistically.

Ammonia has two roles in Tollens reagent: it complexes silver ions and it keeps the solution alkaline for the reduction. Without ammonia, silver oxide would precipitate instead and no mirror would form.
The mirror itself is diagnostic because it requires a clean, smooth surface and a reducing agent strong enough to deposit metal slowly. Fast reduction gives a black powder instead.
A candidate who writes the aldehyde as the reductant in both equations connects the two tests mechanistically.
bullets: Tollens: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ reduced to a silver mirror.
Fehling: Cu(II) blue reduced to red Cu₂O.
The aldehyde is the reductant in both.
Ketones fail both — no oxidation possible.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in carbonyl chemistry
paragraphs: The classic trap is the family name. Alkanals end in -al, alkanones in -one, and the end/middle position follows the suffix. Any option naming ethanal a ketone misreads the structure.

The second trap is the test direction. The silver mirror and the red precipitate both confirm aldehydes; their absence confirms ketones. Candidates who assign the mirror to ketones reverse the distinction.
The third trap is oxidation products. Aldehydes oxidise to carboxylic acids; ketones do not oxidise at all under these conditions. Any option oxidising a ketone to an acid is false.
The fourth trap is the carbonyl carbon's hydrogen. Counting it settles every question in the topic: present means aldehyde, absent means ketone.
A final trap is methanal. Formaldehyde has no alkyl group on the carbonyl carbon at all, which makes it the most reactive aldehyde and the one most likely to be asked about by name.
A candidate who counts the carbonyl hydrogen before reading the options eliminates half the distractors instantly.
It also pays off in every later family.
bullets: -al = aldehyde (end); -one = ketone (middle).
Mirror and red precipitate mean aldehyde.
Ketones never oxidise to acids here.
Count the carbonyl hydrogen first.

lessons.title: Alkanoic Acids and Alkanoates
lessons.objective: Compare the various types of alkanoic acids, infer the products of alkanoic acids and alkanols, identify natural sources of alkanoates, specify the methods for the production of soap, detergent and margarine, and distinguish between detergent and soap.

content.heading: Alkanoic Acids and Alkanoates
paragraphs: Vinegar stings, soap cleans, and margarine spreads — three familiar things from one family of compounds. This lesson follows the alkanoic acids from their reactions to the soaps and fats they build.

content.heading: Alkanoic acids: reactions and types
paragraphs: Alkanoic acids carry the carboxyl group (–COOH): ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) is vinegar; propanoic acid is its next member. They are weak acids — they ionise partly — but they neutralise bases like any acid, forming alkanoates (salts).

Esterification is their signature reaction: a carboxylic acid plus an alkanol gives an ester plus water. Ethanoic acid + ethanol ⇌ ethyl ethanoate + water. The product smells fruity — esters are the perfumes of nature.
Ethanedioic (oxalic) acid is a dicarboxylic acid — two COOH groups on one molecule. Benzoic acid (benzene carboxylic acid) is aromatic, a preservative because it stops microbes growing.
bullets: Alkanoic acids: –COOH, weak acids, form alkanoate salts.
Esterification: acid + alkanol ⇌ ester + water (fruity).
Oxalic acid has two COOH groups; benzoic acid is aromatic.
content.takeaway: Alkanoic acids are weak acids that esterify with alkanols and salt with bases.

check.question: Esterification is the reaction between
options: An alkanoic acid and an alkanol
check.why: Esterification joins an acid and an alkanol, losing water.

content.heading: Fats, oils and alkanoates
paragraphs: Fats and oils are alkanoates: esters of fatty acids with glycerol, a trihydric alkanol. That is why glycerol is both a fat component and a soap by-product. The fatty acid chains decide the fat's firmness — saturated chains pack tight (butter), unsaturated chains stay soft (oils).

Saponification is the alkaline hydrolysis of fats: fat + NaOH → soap + glycerol. Sodium stearate is the soap. Margarine is made by hydrogenating vegetable oils — adding hydrogen across their double bonds hardens them.

Soaps clean by emulsifying grease into micelles that rinse away. Detergents are synthetic sulfonates that clean the same way but do not form scum with hard water. Soap fails in hard water; detergents do not.
bullets: Fats/oils: glycerol esters of fatty acids (alkanoates).
Saponification: fat + NaOH → soap + glycerol.
Margarine: hydrogenated vegetable oil.
Soap scums with hard water; detergents do not.
content.takeaway: Fats are glycerol esters; saponification turns them into soap.

check.question: Saponification of a fat with sodium hydroxide produces
check.why: Alkaline hydrolysis of fats gives soap (alkanoate) plus glycerol.

content.heading: Natural sources and the soap–detergent choice
paragraphs: Alkanoates come from natural fats and oils: palm oil, coconut oil, groundnut oil and animal tallow. The fatty acid composition of each source decides the soap's hardness and lathering.

Soap cleans by the same emulsifying trick as detergent, but it forms insoluble scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ in hard water. Detergents (synthetic sulfonates) form soluble salts and keep working in hard water.
That difference is the whole commercial choice: soap where water is soft, detergent where water is hard. Chemistry decides the market.
bullets: Sources: palm, coconut, groundnut oils; tallow.
Soap scums in hard water; detergents do not.
Choice follows the water, not the brand.
content.takeaway: Soap and detergent clean alike, but only detergent survives hard water.

check.question: Detergents are preferred over soap in hard water because
options: Their salts stay soluble with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺
check.why: Detergent salts are soluble in hard water; soap forms scum.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For ester questions, write the acid and the alkanol first. The ester name combines them: ethyl from the alkanol, ethanoate from the acid.

content.problem: Ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol to form an ester. Write the equation and calculate the mass of ester from 6.0 g of ethanoic acid. (Mr ethanoic acid = 60, Mr ethyl ethanoate = 88)

steps.reason: Acid plus alkanol gives ester plus water
Moles = mass ÷ Mr
One mole of acid gives one mole of ester

content.question: 3.0 g of ethanoic acid is esterified completely with excess ethanol. Calculate the ester mass. (Mr acid = 60, ester = 88)

content.heading: Go deeper: Esterification as equilibrium
paragraphs: Esterification is reversible: the ester hydrolyses back to acid and alkanol in water. The equilibrium lies near the middle, so the yield is never complete without tricks — excess alkanol, or removal of water.
Concentrated sulfuric acid catalyses the reaction by protonating the acid, making the carbonyl carbon more attackable. The catalyst speeds both directions equally, as catalysts always do.
That reversibility is why esters hydrolyse in acidic or alkaline conditions in nature: fats in seeds and fruits are esters that enzymes hydrolyse as food stores.
A candidate who sees esterification as equilibrium explains both perfume-making and fat digestion with one idea.
Excess alkanol pushes the equilibrium toward the ester by Le Chatelier: the alkanol is consumed, so more forms. That is why perfume houses use excess alcohol rather than excess acid.
Removing water works the same way from the other side. Distilling the ester away as it forms drags the equilibrium forward completely.
A candidate who sees the perfume process as equilibrium management understands both the factory and the exam item from one principle.
bullets: Esterification is reversible; yield needs excess or water removal.
Conc. H₂SO₄ catalyses both directions.
Enzymes hydrolyse fats the same way in the body.
One equilibrium explains perfumes and digestion.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why soap fails in hard water
paragraphs: Soap anions pair with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ to form insoluble scum instead of micelles. The soap is wasted on the hardness ions before it can clean. That is the whole chemistry of the hard-water problem.
Detergent sulfonates form soluble calcium salts, so they keep cleaning. The difference is solubility of the salt, nothing more mysterious.
Saponification's glycerol by-product is itself valuable in soaps. A fat plus alkali gives two products, and both are sold — the process wastes nothing.
A candidate who links scum to solubility predicts the soap–detergent choice for any water hardness.
Boiling water soap solution does not remove the scum, because the calcium salts are insoluble at any temperature. Only a chemical exchange — washing soda or resins — removes the hardness ions.
That is why hard-water areas adopted detergents first: the chemistry of scum made soap uneconomic there long before brands competed.
That solubility difference, not cleaning power, is the entire basis of the soap–detergent choice in any water.
It also explains why hard-water areas adopted detergents first of all in history.
bullets: Soap + Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ → insoluble scum.
Detergent salts stay soluble in hard water.
Saponification sells both soap and glycerol.
Solubility of the salt decides the choice.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in acids and alkanoates
paragraphs: The classic trap is the ester name. The first part (-yl) comes from the alkanol; the second (-anoate) from the acid. Ethyl ethanoate is ethanol's ethyl plus ethanoic acid's ethanoate — reversing them names the wrong ester.
The second trap is saponification direction. Alkaline hydrolysis of a fat gives soap plus glycerol; esterification is the reverse. The reagents decide which way the arrow runs.
The third trap is oxalic acid. It is dicarboxylic (two COOH groups), so it neutralises two moles of base per mole. Counting COOH groups settles every stoichiometry item.
The fourth trap is margarine manufacture. It is hydrogenation of vegetable oils, not esterification and not saponification. The double bonds tell the process.
A final trap is the weak-acid label. Alkanoic acids are weak — they ionise partly — but they still neutralise bases fully at the mole ratio. Weak describes ionisation, not neutralisation capacity.
bullets: Ester name: -yl from alkanol, -anoate from acid.
Saponification: fat + alkali → soap + glycerol.
Oxalic acid has two COOH groups.
Margarine is hydrogenation, not esterification.

lessons.title: Amines
lessons.objective: Compare the various classes of alkanamines and classify primary, secondary and tertiary amines.

content.heading: Amines
paragraphs: The rotten-fish smell of a fish market is an amine — a family of compounds with nitrogen at the centre. This lesson names their three classes and the reactions that tell them apart.

content.heading: Primary, secondary and tertiary
paragraphs: Amines carry the amino group (–NH₂) on carbon, like the hydroxyl group of alkanols. The class depends on how many carbons share the nitrogen: primary (1°) amines have one carbon on nitrogen (ethanamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂); secondary (2°) have two (dimethylamine); tertiary (3°) have three (trimethylamine).

That count decides the reactions. Primary amines react with nitrous acid (HNO₂) to give nitrogen gas, which is their distinguishing test. Secondary amines give a yellow oil with the same reagent, and tertiary amines do not react at all.
Amines are bases: they accept protons to form ammonium-type ions. That basicity makes them smell fishy and makes their salts soluble in water.
bullets: 1°: one C on N. 2°: two C. 3°: three C.
Primary + HNO₂ → N₂ gas (distinguishing test).
Amines are bases; the lone pair accepts protons.
content.takeaway: Count the carbons on nitrogen to name the class; primary amines fizz with nitrous acid.

check.question: Ethylamine (CH₃CH₂NH₂) is a primary amine because its nitrogen is bonded to
check.why: One carbon on the nitrogen makes it primary.

content.heading: Reactions and the nitrous acid test
paragraphs: The distinguishing test uses nitrous acid (HNO₂), made in situ from sodium nitrite and dilute hydrochloric acid. Primary amines react to give nitrogen gas — visible effervescence — plus an alcohol.

Secondary amines give a yellow oil (an N-nitroso compound) that does not bubble. Tertiary amines give no reaction with cold nitrous acid. The three results are three different answers to the same reagent.
The nitrogen gas from a primary amine is quantitative: moles of gas equal moles of amine. That makes the reaction both a test and a measurement.
bullets: Primary: N₂ effervescence with HNO₂.
Secondary: yellow oil, no gas.
Tertiary: no reaction in the cold.
content.takeaway: Nitrous acid separates all three classes: gas, oil, or nothing.

check.question: A primary amine with cold nitrous acid gives
check.why: Primary amines react with HNO₂ to liberate nitrogen gas.

content.heading: Properties and uses
paragraphs: Amines are polar, hydrogen-bonding compounds, soluble in water when small. Their smell is a warning system: trimethylamine is the rotten-fish smell of decaying fish, because bacteria produce it from choline.
They undergo salt formation with acids, alkylation with halogenoalkanes, and acylation — the reactions that build dyes, drugs and polyamides (nylon). The lone pair does all of it.
Aniline, the aromatic amine, is the parent of the dye industry. The whole dye and pharmaceutical world grew from amine chemistry.
That lone pair also makes amines smell strongly and react with many reagents, so they are stored sealed and handled with care.
bullets: Polar, water-soluble when small; fishy smell.
Salt formation, alkylation, acylation reactions.
Aniline parents the dye industry.
content.takeaway: Amines are basic, fishy-smelling, and the parents of dyes and drugs.

check.question: The rotten-fish smell of decaying fish is caused by
check.why: Bacteria produce trimethylamine, an amine, as fish decays.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For amine questions, count the carbons on nitrogen first. The count (1, 2 or 3) predicts the nitrous acid result before any reagent is named.

content.problem: 0.1 mol of a primary amine reacts with excess nitrous acid. Calculate the volume of nitrogen gas at s.t.p. liberated.

steps.reason: Primary amine plus nitrous acid gives nitrogen and an alcohol
One mole of amine gives one mole of N₂
One mole of gas fills 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.

content.question: 0.2 mol of a primary amine reacts with excess nitrous acid. Calculate the nitrogen volume at s.t.p.
hints: One mole of amine gives one mole of N₂

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the classes differ
paragraphs: The reaction with nitrous acid needs a replaceable hydrogen on nitrogen. Primary amines carry two, so diazotisation proceeds to nitrogen gas. Secondary amines carry one, so they stop at the yellow oil. Tertiary amines carry none, so nothing happens.
That single count — hydrogens on nitrogen — predicts the test result for every class. It is the amine version of the alkanol reactivity ladder.

Basicity follows a related but different order, because alkyl groups donate electron density and stabilise the ammonium ion. Basic strength and diazotisation rate are different ladders and must not be merged.
A candidate who counts hydrogens for the test and electron donation for basicity keeps the two ladders separate.

Basicity rises with alkyl substitution because the groups donate electron density and stabilise the ammonium ion. Greater donation means a stronger base, which is why trimethylamine is more basic than methylamine.
That donation order is not the diazotisation order. A candidate who ranks basicity by the test result merges two different ladders and loses both items.
A candidate who counts hydrogens for the test and electron donation for basicity keeps the two ladders separate.
It also pays off in every later amine family.
bullets: Diazotisation needs N–H hydrogen: 1° has two, 2° has one, 3° none.
Basicity follows electron donation — a different order.
Two ladders, never merged.
Count hydrogens for the test.

content.heading: Go deeper: Diazotisation and dyes
paragraphs: Diazotisation is the conversion of a primary aromatic amine (aniline) with nitrous acid at low temperature into a diazonium salt. That salt couples with other aromatics to form azo dyes — the largest dye family in the world.
The reaction must stay cold because diazonium salts decompose on warming. Temperature control is part of the chemistry, not a detail.
Aliphatic diazonium salts are unstable and decompose at once to nitrogen gas — which is why the test works for aliphatic amines. Aromatic ones survive long enough to couple.
The same reaction thus tests aliphatic amines and manufactures aromatic dyes. Stability of the intermediate decides which use.
The coupling step is electrophilic substitution on the aromatic ring, so the diazonium ion is the electrophile. Electron-donating groups on the coupling partner speed it up.
That mechanism links amines to the whole dye industry: diazotisation plus coupling is the manufacturing sequence for azo colours.
A candidate who knows the diazonium must be kept cold answers both the test item and the dye item from one fact.
bullets: Aniline + HNO₂ (cold) → diazonium salt → azo dyes.
Aliphatic diazonium salts decompose instantly (N₂ test).
Cold temperature is essential for diazotisation.
One reaction, two industries.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in amines
paragraphs: The classic trap is the class count. The carbons on nitrogen decide: ethanamine is primary, dimethylamine secondary, trimethylamine tertiary. Counting total carbons instead of nitrogen neighbours misnames every case.
The second trap is the test direction. Nitrogen gas means primary; yellow oil means secondary; nothing means tertiary. Any option assigning nitrogen gas to a secondary amine reverses the test.
The third trap is the amine versus amide confusion. Amides are carboxamides (CONH₂), amines are alkylamines (RNH₂). The -amide and -amine endings are different families entirely.
The fourth trap is basicity versus test order. Basic strength does not follow the diazotisation order; merging the two ladders loses both items.
A final trap is calling ammonia an amine. Ammonia is the parent of the family, not a member — it has no carbon at all.
bullets: Count carbons on nitrogen, not total carbons.
N₂ = primary; yellow oil = secondary; nothing = tertiary.
Amides (CONH₂) ≠ amines (RNH₂).
Basicity and test orders are different ladders.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates
lessons.objective: Identify natural sources of carbohydrates, compare the various classes of carbohydrates, infer the products of hydrolysis and dehydration of carbohydrates, determine the uses of carbohydrates, and specify the tests for simple sugars.

content.heading: Carbohydrates
paragraphs: Bread, yam, rice and sugar are all carbohydrates — the foods that feed most of the world. This lesson sorts them by size and follows them through the tests and the reactions that matter.

content.heading: Mono-, di- and polysaccharides
paragraphs: Carbohydrates are compounds of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, usually in the ratio CH₂O. They are classified by size: monosaccharides are single units (glucose, fructose), disaccharides are pairs (sucrose, lactose, maltose), and polysaccharides are long chains (starch, cellulose).

Glucose and fructose are reducing sugars: they reduce Fehling's solution to red copper(I) oxide. Sucrose is non-reducing until it is hydrolysed. The reducing test therefore finds single units but misses paired ones.
Cellulose from cotton is the most abundant organic polymer on earth; starch from cassava is its food-store relative. Both are polysaccharides, but humans digest starch and not cellulose.
bullets: Mono-: glucose, fructose. Di-: sucrose, lactose, maltose.
Poly-: starch, cellulose.
Reducing sugars (glucose, fructose) reduce Fehling's; sucrose does not.
content.takeaway: Size classifies carbohydrates: single, pairs, or chains.

check.question: Which of these is a disaccharide?
check.why: Sucrose is two sugar units joined; glucose and fructose are single.

content.heading: Tests for sugars and hydrolysis
paragraphs: The Fehling test finds reducing sugars: a blue solution that turns red with red copper(I) oxide on warming. Benedict's solution works the same way. Sucrose fails the test until it is hydrolysed into glucose and fructose.

Hydrolysis breaks complex sugars into simple ones: sucrose + water → glucose + fructose (with dilute acid); starch → maltose → glucose. Cellulose resists hydrolysis, which is why humans cannot digest it.
Concentrated tetraoxosulfate(VI) acid dehydrates sugars: glucose chars to black carbon. That dehydration is the test that distinguishes sugars from non-carbohydrates.
bullets: Fehling: blue → red Cu₂O with reducing sugars.
Sucrose hydrolyses to glucose + fructose.
Conc. H₂SO₄ dehydrates sugars to carbon.
content.takeaway: Fehling finds reducing sugars; hydrolysis breaks big sugars into small ones.

check.question: Sucrose fails the Fehling test because
check.why: Sucrose has no free aldehyde group; hydrolysis frees glucose and fructose first.

content.heading: Uses of sugar and starch
paragraphs: Sugar and starch feed fermentation for alcoholic beverages: glucose ferments to ethanol. The same fermentation brews palm wine, and distillation raises it to gin. Carbohydrates thus feed both food and drink industries.
Starch is used in pharmaceuticals (as a binder and filler), in textiles (sizing), and in paper manufacture. Cellulose from cotton is the textile fibre itself — the largest natural fibre industry.
The uses follow the structure: energy storage (starch), structure (cellulose), and quick energy (sugars). Each class has its own job.
Preservation is a third use: sugar binds water so microbes cannot grow, which is why jam and suya keep without refrigeration.
bullets: Fermentation of glucose → ethanol (drinks, palm wine to gin).
Starch: pharmaceuticals, textiles, paper.
Cellulose: the cotton fibre itself.
content.takeaway: Sugars ferment, starch binds and fills, cellulose clothe us.

check.question: Palm wine becomes gin by
check.why: Yeast ferments the sap to ethanol; distillation concentrates it to gin.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For carbohydrate questions, first ask the size class. Single, pair or chain decides the reaction, the test and the use.

content.problem: Sucrose is hydrolysed to glucose and fructose. Calculate the mass of glucose from 34.2 g of sucrose. (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + C₆H₁₂O₆; Mr sucrose = 342, glucose = 180)

steps.reason: Moles = mass ÷ Mr
One mole of sucrose gives one mole of glucose
Mass = moles × Mr

content.question: 17.1 g of sucrose is hydrolysed completely. Calculate the glucose mass formed. (Mr = 342 and 180)

content.heading: Go deeper: Why sucrose is non-reducing
paragraphs: A reducing sugar needs a free aldehyde (or keto) group to reduce Fehling's solution. In glucose that group is free; in sucrose the two units are joined through their reactive groups, so the aldehyde is locked away. Joining hides the reactivity.
Hydrolysis frees the groups again, which is why hydrolysed sucrose then reduces Fehling's. The test result changes because the structure changed, not because the atoms did.
That is why the syllabus pairs the test with hydrolysis: the sequence — test, hydrolyse, test again — proves the structure. A candidate who runs the sequence explains sucrose completely.
Maltose and lactose are reducing because their join leaves one unit's group free. The exception proves the rule: it is the free group, not the size, that decides.

The same joining logic explains why maltose and lactose stay reducing: their structures link one unit through a different carbon, leaving one reactive group free. It is the position of the join that matters, not the fact of joining.
A candidate who pictures the join can predict the test result for any disaccharide without memorising it.
A candidate who pictures the join can predict the test result for any disaccharide without memorising it.
It also pays off in every later family.
It also pays off in every later family of reactions.
bullets: Reducing power needs a free aldehyde/keto group.
Sucrose locks both groups in the join.
Hydrolysis frees them — the test then works.
Maltose/lactose stay reducing (one group free).

content.heading: Go deeper: Starch, cellulose and the digestion difference
paragraphs: Starch and cellulose are both glucose polymers, but their links differ: starch is alpha-linked and enzymes cut it easily, while cellulose is beta-linked in straight chains that humans have no enzyme to break. Structure, not composition, decides digestibility.
That is why grass-fed animals digest cellulose through gut bacteria: the bacteria supply the enzyme humans lack. The polymer is the same; the machinery differs.
The same link difference drives industry: starch is food and pulp, cellulose is fibre and paper. One polymer feeds, the other clothes.
A candidate who names the link type (alpha versus beta) has explained digestion, textiles and industry from one idea.

The link difference also decides industrial treatment: starch gelatinises in hot water and feeds fermentation, while cellulose must be pulped mechanically because no enzyme in the factory breaks it either.
That is why paper is made from cellulose and bread from starch. One polymer feeds; the other clothes and writes.
bullets: Starch: alpha-linked, digestible. Cellulose: beta-linked, indigestible.
Ruminants use bacteria to break cellulose.
One polymer feeds; the other clothes.
The link type is the whole explanation.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in carbohydrates
paragraphs: The classic trap is the reducing test. Glucose and fructose reduce Fehling's; sucrose does not until hydrolysed. Any option giving sucrose a positive test without hydrolysis reverses the chemistry.
The second trap is starch versus cellulose digestibility. Both are glucose polymers, but only starch is digestible. Composition alone never decides — the link type does.
The third trap is dehydration. Concentrated sulfuric acid chars sugars to carbon; it is a dehydration, not an oxidation. The black residue is carbon, not ash.
The fourth trap is fermentation direction. Yeast converts sugar to ethanol, never the reverse. Any option making ethanol the fermented product's starting material reverses the process.
A final trap is the sugar source. Reducing sugars occur in fruits and honey; cassava and yam store starch. The natural source names the class, and the class names the reaction.
bullets: Sucrose is non-reducing until hydrolysed.
Alpha links digest; beta links do not.
Conc. H₂SO₄ dehydrates sugars to carbon.
Fermentation: sugar → ethanol, never backwards.

lessons.title: Proteins and Enzymes
lessons.objective: Identify the basic structure of proteins, specify the methods and products of hydrolysis, specify the various tests for proteins, and state the functions of enzymes.

content.heading: Proteins and Enzymes
paragraphs: Meat, eggs, beans and milk all share one building material: protein. This lesson explains what proteins are, how tests find them, and the tiny workers — enzymes — that build and break them.

content.heading: The structure of proteins
paragraphs: Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Twenty amino acids make all proteins; their sequence and folding decide the protein's shape and job. Insulin, haemoglobin and keratin are all amino-acid chains folded differently.

Primary structure is the amino-acid sequence. Secondary structure is the local folding into helices and sheets. Tertiary structure is the whole chain folded into a three-dimensional shape — and the shape is the function.
Denaturation unfolds the shape: heat or acid destroys it, and the protein loses its job. Boiling an egg white is denaturation made visible.
bullets: Proteins = amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
Structure: sequence → helix/sheet → 3D fold → function.
Denaturation unfolds the shape and kills the function.
content.takeaway: Sequence folds into shape, and shape is the protein's job.

check.question: The primary structure of a protein is
check.why: Primary structure is the order of amino acids in the chain.

content.heading: Hydrolysis and the protein tests
paragraphs: Hydrolysis breaks proteins back into amino acids: acid hydrolysis (hot HCl) or enzyme hydrolysis (digestion). The products are the same amino acids the protein was built from — hydrolysis reverses polymerisation.

The biuret test finds peptide bonds: copper(II) sulfate in alkali gives a violet colour. The ninhydrin test finds amino groups: ninhydrin gives a blue-purple colour. Millon's test finds tyrosine through its phenolic OH group: Millon's reagent (mercury(II) nitrate in nitric acid) gives a red colour.

The xanthoproteic test finds aromatic rings: concentrated nitric acid nitrates the rings to give a yellow colour that turns orange with alkali. Each test targets a different feature — bonds, amino groups, or rings.
bullets: Hydrolysis: protein → amino acids (acid or enzymes).
Biuret: violet with CuSO₄/alkali (peptide bonds).
Ninhydrin: blue-purple (amino groups). Millon: red (phenolic OH of tyrosine).
Xanthoproteic: yellow → orange (aromatic rings).
content.takeaway: Hydrolysis reverses building; each test targets a different feature.

check.question: The biuret test for proteins gives
check.why: Biuret reagent (CuSO₄ in alkali) gives a violet colour with peptide bonds.

content.heading: Enzymes and their functions
paragraphs: Enzymes are biological catalysts — proteins that speed reactions without being used up. Amylase breaks starch in the mouth and gut; pepsin breaks proteins in the stomach; catalase breaks hydrogen peroxide in cells.
Enzymes work by lowering the activation energy: they provide a surface where reactants meet in the right orientation. They do not change the equilibrium or the final yield — only the speed.
Enzymes are specific: each fits particular substrates, like a lock and key. Temperature and pH control them — heat denatures them, and extreme pH changes their shape, killing their function.
bullets: Enzymes are protein catalysts, unchanged by the reaction.
They lower activation energy; they never change yield.
Specific (lock and key); destroyed by heat and extreme pH.
content.takeaway: Enzymes are specific protein catalysts that lower the energy hill.

check.question: An enzyme speeds a reaction by
check.why: Enzymes lower the activation energy, so more collisions succeed.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For protein questions, first ask which feature the test targets: bonds (biuret), amino groups (ninhydrin), or rings (xanthoproteic). The feature names the test.

content.problem: A peptide bond links two amino acids. Calculate the number of peptide bonds in a protein of 100 amino acids.

steps.reason: Amino acids join end to end like beads on a string
Each new amino acid adds one peptide bond
A chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds

content.question: A protein has 50 amino acids in one chain. How many peptide bonds does it contain?
hints: Each amino acid after the first adds one bond

content.heading: Go deeper: Why shape is function
paragraphs: A protein's shape decides its job: haemoglobin's pocket cradles oxygen, enzymes' clefts fit their substrates, keratin's helices make hair tough. Denaturation unfolds the shape, and the job stops even though the sequence is unchanged.
That is why boiling an egg white matters: the protein is still there, but unfolded. Function lives in the fold, not the formula.
Enzymes exploit the same principle: their active sites are shaped for specific substrates. A wrong shape means no reaction — specificity is geometry.
A candidate who links sequence → fold → function explains every protein question in the syllabus from one chain.
The same folding logic explains why some proteins are fibres (keratin in hair and nails) and others are globular (haemoglobin in blood). Fibres need strength; globular proteins need pockets.
A candidate who pictures the fold can predict the job: long fibres for strength, compact globules for carrying and catalysis.
A candidate who links sequence to fold to function explains every protein question in the syllabus from one chain of reasoning.
It also pays off in every later structural question, from enzymes to fibres.
That chain of reasoning is the whole topic in one line.
bullets: Shape decides the job: pockets, clefts, fibres.
Denaturation unfolds without breaking the sequence.
Enzyme specificity is geometry (lock and key).
One chain: sequence → fold → function.

content.heading: Go deeper: How enzymes lower the hill
paragraphs: An enzyme provides an active site where reactants bind in the right orientation, which lowers the activation energy. The reaction then proceeds at body temperature instead of needing heat.
Because the enzyme is unchanged, it works again and again: one amylase molecule digests thousands of starch molecules. That turnover is why tiny amounts of enzyme do large jobs.
The enzyme never changes the equilibrium or the yield. It only changes the speed. Any option giving an enzyme control over the final amount reverses its role.
Heat and pH kill enzymes by denaturing them — unfolding the active site. That is why fever denatures and why cooking kills bacteria: the workers are unfolded.
Inhibitors exploit the same site: competitive inhibitors block it, non-competitive ones change its shape. Drugs are designed as enzyme inhibitors for exactly this reason.
The lock-and-key picture thus covers catalysis, inhibition and denaturation in one image. Few models in the syllabus work this hard.
bullets: Active site lowers activation energy by orientation.
One enzyme, thousands of reactions (turnover).
Enzymes never change yield or equilibrium.
Heat and pH denature — unfolding kills function.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in proteins
paragraphs: The classic trap is the test–feature match. Biuret targets peptide bonds, ninhydrin targets amino groups, Millon targets tyrosine, xanthoproteic targets aromatic rings. Naming the feature first prevents every mismatch.

The second trap is denaturation versus hydrolysis. Denaturation unfolds the protein (function lost, sequence kept); hydrolysis breaks the sequence (amino acids freed). The two processes are different depths of destruction.
The third trap is the enzyme's role. Enzymes speed reactions without changing yield or equilibrium. Any option giving an enzyme control over the final amount reverses its role.
The fourth trap is the peptide bond count. A chain of n amino acids has n − 1 bonds, not n. The first amino acid adds no bond — it starts the chain.
A final trap is the hydrolysis product. Acid hydrolysis of a protein gives amino acids, not sugars. Any option releasing glucose from a protein confuses the two polymer families.
bullets: Match each test to its feature before answering.
Denaturation unfolds; hydrolysis breaks the chain.
Enzymes never change yield or equilibrium.
n amino acids = n − 1 peptide bonds.

lessons.title: Polymers
lessons.objective: Distinguish between natural and synthetic polymers, differentiate between addition and condensation polymerization processes, classify natural and commercial polymers and their uses, and distinguish between thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics.

content.heading: Polymers
paragraphs: A plastic bucket, a nylon shirt and a rubber tyre share one trick: thousands of small molecules joined into one giant chain. This lesson explains how the chains form and why some melt while others never do.

content.heading: Addition versus condensation
paragraphs: Addition polymerisation links monomers through their double bonds, with no by-product: ethene chains link into polythene, styrene into polystyrene. The reaction is addition repeated thousands of times.

Condensation polymerisation joins monomers with small molecules lost: amino acids lose water to form proteins, and dicarboxylic acids with diols lose water to form polyesters like terylene. Nylon is a condensation polymer too.
The distinction is the by-product: addition loses nothing; condensation loses water (or alcohol). The equation shows it at a glance.
The by-product is the quickest check of all: look at the equation, and if water appears, the polymerisation was condensation.
Polymer length matters too: longer chains mean stronger, tougher plastics because more entanglement holds them together. That is why molecular weight is controlled so carefully in manufacture.
bullets: Addition: monomers link through double bonds; nothing lost.
Condensation: monomers join with water or alcohol lost.
Add: polythene, polystyrene. Condense: nylon, terylene, proteins.
content.takeaway: Addition loses nothing; condensation loses water.

check.question: Nylon is a condensation polymer because its formation
check.why: Condensation polymers form with small molecules lost, like water.

content.heading: Natural and synthetic polymers
paragraphs: Natural polymers come from living things: cellulose (cotton, wood), proteins (wool, silk), starch and natural rubber. They are made by biology, not factories, though humans process them.
Synthetic polymers are made by chemical plants: polythene, PVC, polystyrene, nylon, terylene and synthetic rubber. They are designed for specific properties — strength, insulation, flexibility.
The class decides the fate: natural polymers are biodegradable and renewable; synthetic ones persist and accumulate. That environmental difference is now part of every use decision.
Synthetic rubber, for example, copies the properties of natural rubber from petroleum feedstock. The category is about origin, not about performance.
bullets: Natural: cellulose, proteins, starch, natural rubber.
Synthetic: polythene, PVC, nylon, terylene, synthetic rubber.
Natural biodegrades; synthetic persists.
content.takeaway: Natural polymers come from living things; synthetic ones from reactors.

check.question: Which of these is a natural polymer?
check.why: Cellulose is the plant polymer found in cotton and wood.

content.heading: Thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics
paragraphs: Thermoplastics soften on heating and harden on cooling, again and again: polythene, polystyrene, PVC. They can be remelted and remoulded, which makes them recyclable — and disposable.
Thermosetting plastics harden once and never soften again: Bakelite and melamine set by cross-linking into a rigid network. Heating them further chars them instead of melting them.
The difference is cross-linking: thermoplastics are individual chains that slide; thermosets are one interlocked network. Structure decides whether remelting is possible.
That is why a broken thermoplastic bucket can be remelted into a new bucket, while a broken thermoset switch cannot be recovered at all.
bullets: Thermoplastics: remelt and remould (polythene, PVC).
Thermosets: harden once, never remelt (Bakelite).
Cross-linking decides the difference.
content.takeaway: Thermoplastics remelt; thermosets set once and char.

check.question: Bakelite is a thermosetting plastic because
options: It hardens once and cannot be remelted
check.why: Thermosets cross-link permanently; reheating chars them instead of softening.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For polymer questions, first check for a by-product: water lost means condensation, nothing lost means addition. The equation tells the class.

content.problem: Ethene polymerises to polythene. Write the polymerisation equation and state whether it is addition or condensation.

steps.reason: Polythene is made from ethene monomers
Double bonds open and join thousands of units
No small molecule is lost

content.question: Amino acids join to form proteins with water lost at each join. Classify the polymerisation.
hints: Small molecules are lost at each join

content.heading: Go deeper: Why thermoplastics remelt and thermosets do not
paragraphs: A thermoplastic is a pile of individual chains held together only by weak forces. Heating weakens those forces, so the chains slide and the plastic flows; cooling restores them. The chains themselves never change.
A thermoset is one giant network: cross-links join the chains into a single molecule. Heating cannot slide what is interlocked, so the material chars instead of melting. The network is the molecule.
That structural difference is why thermoplastics can be recycled and thermosets cannot. Remelting is always a chain-separation question.
A candidate who pictures piles versus networks predicts remelting, hardness and recyclability for any polymer.

The same picture explains recycled plastics: thermoplastics are ground and remelted because their chains survive the process, while thermosets must be ground into filler because their networks cannot flow.
Even the filler market follows the picture: ground thermoset powder is used as a cheap filler precisely because it cannot flow back into shape.
Cross-link density controls hardness directly: more links mean a harder, more brittle network. That is why Bakelite is rigid while lightly cross-linked rubber stays flexible.
The same density also governs heat resistance: heavily cross-linked networks keep their shape where thermoplastics would soften. Structure, again, is destiny.
bullets: Thermoplastics: separate chains, weak forces, remelt.
Thermosets: one interlocked network, chars.
Structure decides remelting and recycling.
Piles versus networks is the whole distinction.

content.heading: Go deeper: Vulcanised rubber and cross-linking
paragraphs: Natural rubber is polyisoprene chains, too soft and sticky for tyres. Vulcanisation heats it with sulfur, which forms cross-links between chains. The network makes it hard, elastic and durable.
Synthetic rubber is made the same way from synthetic monomers: the cross-linking step is identical, only the starting chains differ. Vulcanisation is a treatment, not a polymerisation.
The cross-links also explain why vulcanised rubber cannot be remelted: heating breaks the network, it does not slide it. Rubber is a thermoset once vulcanised.
A candidate who separates polymerisation (making chains) from vulcanisation (linking them) keeps two processes distinct.
The sulfur bridges also explain the smell of hot rubber and the ageing of tyres: heat breaks some bridges over time, and the network weakens.
Synthetic rubber follows the same treatment: Buna-S and neoprene are vulcanised exactly like natural rubber, proving that cross-linking is independent of the chain source.
bullets: Vulcanisation cross-links rubber chains with sulfur.
Same treatment for natural and synthetic rubber.
Vulcanised rubber is thermoset — it chars, not melts.
Polymerisation makes chains; vulcanisation links them.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in polymers
paragraphs: The classic trap is the by-product. Addition loses nothing; condensation loses water or alcohol. Any option describing amino acids joining without water lost is addition, not condensation.
The second trap is natural versus synthetic. Cellulose is natural; nylon is synthetic. Both are polymers, but only one comes from living things.
The third trap is thermoplastic versus thermosetting. Remelting means thermoplastic; charring means thermosetting. The heating test decides, not the softness.
The fourth trap is vulcanisation as polymerisation. Sulfur cross-links existing chains; it does not make them. The two processes are sequential, not the same.
A final trap is calling natural rubber synthetic because tyres are manufactured. Origin decides the category: natural rubber comes from latex, however it is processed afterwards.
A candidate who checks the by-product, the heating test, and the origin in that order answers every polymer item without memorising examples.
That order — by-product, heating, origin — is the whole polymer method in one line.
bullets: By-product decides: water = condensation; nothing = addition.
Natural = living; synthetic = reactor-made.
Remelts = thermoplastic; chars = thermosetting.
Vulcanisation links chains; it does not make them.

lessons.title: Transition Metals
lessons.objective: Identify the general properties of the first transition metals, deduce reasons for electron configuration, oxidation states, complex ion formation, coloured ions and catalysis.

content.heading: Transition Metals
paragraphs: Iron, copper, zinc and their neighbours in the middle of the periodic table do things ordinary metals do not: they form coloured solutions, change their oxidation state, and speed up reactions without being used up. This lesson explains why the middle of the table is special.

content.heading: Electron configuration and variable oxidation states
paragraphs: Transition metals fill an inner d-subshell after the s-subshell: iron is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. Because the s and d electrons have similar energy, they are lost together. Iron can lose two electrons to become Fe²⁺ or three to become Fe³⁺.

That loss of both subshells gives variable oxidation states: manganese goes from +2 to +7, iron from +2 to +3, copper from +1 to +2. Main-group metals have one fixed state; transition metals have several.
The inner d-subshell, partly filled, is also why they form complex ions and coloured compounds. A partly filled d-block is the whole explanation in one phrase.
bullets: Fill order: 4s then 3d — iron is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶.
Loss of 4s and 3d gives variable oxidation states.
Partly filled d-subshell explains colour and complexes.
content.takeaway: Inner d electrons give transition metals variable states and colour.

check.question: Iron forms Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ because
options: It gains electrons in two steps
It can lose electrons from both 4s and 3d subshells
It has two shells of electrons
It reacts with two different acids
check.why: Both the 4s and 3d electrons can be lost, giving two common oxidation states.

content.heading: Complex ions and coloured solutions
paragraphs: Transition metals form complex ions because their partly filled d-orbitals can accept lone pairs from ligands. Copper(II) with ammonia gives [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺, deep blue; iron(III) with thiocyanate gives a blood-red complex.

The colour comes from electron jumps within the split d-orbitals: ligands split the d-levels, and absorbed light energy matches the split. Different ligands split differently, so the same metal gives different colours — copper(II) is blue in water, deep blue in ammonia, green in chloride.
Colour is therefore a ligand effect, not a metal effect alone. The same Cu²⁺ is blue, green or deep blue depending on what surrounds it.
bullets: Ligands donate lone pairs into empty d-orbitals.
Colour = electron jumps across the ligand-split d-levels.
Same metal, different ligands, different colours.
content.takeaway: Ligands split the d-levels; the split decides the colour.

check.question: Copper(II) is blue in water but deep blue in excess ammonia because
options: Different ligands split the d-levels differently
check.why: Ligands split the d-orbitals by different amounts, changing the colour absorbed.

content.heading: Catalysis
paragraphs: Transition metals and their compounds are the best catalysts: iron in the Haber process, vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process, nickel in hydrogenation, platinum in catalytic converters. Their variable oxidation states let them hand electrons back and forth.
A catalyst works by providing a surface where reactants adsorb and the activation energy falls. The metal's partly filled d-orbitals bind reactants temporarily, then release the products unchanged.
That is why transition metals are used as heterogeneous catalysts — solids in gas or liquid reactions. They are recovered and reused, which is the economic point of catalysis.
bullets: Iron (Haber), V₂O₅ (Contact), Ni (hydrogenation), Pt (converters).
Variable states allow electron hand-over.
Heterogeneous catalysts are recovered and reused.
content.takeaway: Variable oxidation states let transition metals work as catalysts.

check.question: Transition metals are good catalysts because
options: They form variable oxidation states and bind reactants
check.why: Variable states let them adsorb reactants, hand over electrons, and release products.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For transition metal questions, first write the electron configuration. The d-block fill explains states, colour and catalysis in one move.

content.problem: Iron is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. Explain why Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ are both common, and write the configuration of Fe³⁺.

steps.operation: List the electrons that can be lost
steps.reason: The 4s and 3d electrons have similar energy, so both can leave
The outer 4s electrons leave before 3d
One more 3d electron leaves

content.question: Copper is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰. Explain why Cu⁺ is less common than Cu²⁺ in aqueous solution.
hints: Write the configurations of Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺
The 3d¹⁰ shell is full and stable, so Cu⁺ disproportionates

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the d-block is special
paragraphs: Main-group metals lose their outer s and p electrons, leaving a noble-gas core. Transition metals lose s and d together, leaving a partly filled d-subshell. That remainder can accept ligands, change colour and hand over electrons one at a time.
The partly filled d-subshell is therefore not a detail but the definition of the family. Every characteristic property — variable states, colour, complexes, catalysis — traces back to it.
That is why zinc, with a full 3d¹⁰ subshell, behaves like a main-group metal: no variable states, no colour, no complex chemistry. The exception proves the d-block rule.
A candidate who writes the configuration first can predict which transition behaviour to expect for any metal.

The same partly filled subshell explains why transition metals have high densities, high melting points and good conductivity: the delocalised d-electrons contribute to the metallic bonding alongside the s-electrons.
A candidate who writes the configuration first can predict which transition behaviour to expect for any metal in the series.
It also pays off in every later transition metal question.
It also pays off in every later transition metal question.
It also pays off in every later transition metal question in the syllabus.
bullets: Partly filled d = transition behaviour.
Main-group metals lose to a noble-gas core.
Zinc (3d¹⁰ full) behaves like a main-group metal.
Configuration first, properties second.

content.heading: Go deeper: Colour from ligand splitting
paragraphs: Ligands split the d-orbitals into two sets with an energy gap. Light of matching energy promotes an electron across the gap; the colour seen is the complement of the colour absorbed.
Stronger ligands split wider, absorbing higher-energy (shorter-wavelength) light. The same Cu²⁺ therefore looks different with water, ammonia or chloride — the ligand sets the gap.
That is why analytical chemistry uses colour as evidence: a deep blue solution is a diagnosis, not a description. The colour reports the complex.
A candidate who links split size to colour seen answers both identification and explanation items from one rule.
Water is a weak ligand, ammonia a stronger one, and chloride a weaker one still. The colour series for copper(II) — pale blue, deep blue, green — is the split series read as colour.
That is why analytical tests specify the ligand: a colour without its ligand is an incomplete observation.

IUPAC names the complex by ligand first, then metal: [Cu(NH3)4]2+ is tetraamminecopper(II), [Fe(CN)6]3- is hexacyanoferrate(III), and [Fe(CN)6]4- is hexacyanoferrate(II). The Roman numeral is the oxidation state; the prefix counts the ligands. Naming the complex is naming the ligand count plus the metal state.
bullets: Ligands split d-orbitals; light promotes electrons across the gap.
Stronger ligands = wider split = higher-energy absorption.
Colour reports the complex present.
One rule explains identification and explanation.
[Cu(NH3)4]2+ = tetraamminecopper(II); [Fe(CN)6]3- = hexacyanoferrate(III).

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in transition metals
paragraphs: The classic trap is the fill order. Transition metals fill 4s before 3d, but lose 4s before 3d when forming ions. Writing the ion's configuration with 3d first reverses the loss order.
The second trap is zinc. Zinc has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell, so it shows no variable states, no colour and no catalytic activity. Calling zinc a typical transition metal fails every item.
The third trap is colour as a metal property. Colour belongs to the complex, not the metal alone. The same Cu²⁺ gives different colours with different ligands.
The fourth trap is catalysis direction. Catalysts speed both directions equally and never change yield or equilibrium. Any option giving a catalyst control over the final amount reverses its role.
A final trap is the oxidation state count. Manganese(VII) in permanganate is +7, not +5, because the sum rule includes the four oxygens at −2 each. Writing the sum prevents the error.
bullets: Fill 4s then 3d; lose 4s then 3d.
Zinc (3d¹⁰) is not a typical transition metal.
Colour belongs to the complex, not the metal.
Catalysts never change yield or equilibrium.

lessons.title: Nitrogen Cycle
lessons.objective: Explain the nitrogen cycle — nitrogen fixation, nitrification, assimilation, denitrification — and examine its relevance to the environment.

content.heading: Nitrogen cycle
paragraphs: Most of the air around us is nitrogen gas, but plants cannot use it directly. The nitrogen cycle is the journey that turns air nitrogen into food for plants and then returns it to the air again.

content.heading: Fixation: locking air nitrogen into the soil
paragraphs: A farmer's beans grow slowly in poor soil because the roots cannot use air nitrogen. Fixation is like charging a battery; hard energy pushes stable nitrogen gas into a form plants can use. Without that charge, the battery stays empty.

Lightning does one kind of fixation high in the sky. Its great heat joins nitrogen and oxygen in air to make nitrogen oxides, and rain carries them down to the soil. The Haber process does fixation in factories, joining nitrogen with hydrogen to make ammonia for fertilisers.
Legume bacteria do fixation inside the soil help. Rhizobium bacteria live in root nodules on beans and peas, so the plant feeds them. In return they turn air nitrogen into ammonia the plant can use.
bullets: Lightning fixation: heat joins nitrogen and oxygen; rain carries oxides down.
Haber fixation: nitrogen plus hydrogen gives ammonia in factories.
Biological fixation: Rhizobium in legume nodules makes ammonia in soil.
content.takeaway: Fixation uses great energy to lock air nitrogen into usable ammonia.

check.question: Which process is fixation?
options: Returning nitrogen gas to the air
check.why: Fixation makes usable ammonia from air nitrogen; the others move nitrogen later.

content.heading: Nitrification and assimilation: feeding the plant
paragraphs: Dead leaves and animal waste rot and release ammonium ions into the soil water. Plants cannot build proteins from ammonium alone, so soil bacteria must pass the nitrogen on. That passing-on work is called nitrification.
Nitrosomonas bacteria change ammonium, NH4+, into nitrite, NO2-. Nitrobacter bacteria then change nitrite into nitrate, NO3-. Nitrate is the main food plants absorb from soil water.

Plants take up nitrate through their roots. Inside the plant, nitrate is changed into amino acids and then into proteins for new leaves and seeds. This uptake and building work is called assimilation.
bullets: Nitrosomonas: NH4+ to NO2- (ammonium to nitrite).
Nitrobacter: NO2- to NO3- (nitrite to nitrate).
Assimilation: plant roots absorb nitrate and build proteins.
Soil nitrate feeds crops but can easily wash away in heavy rain.
content.takeaway: Nitrifying bacteria make nitrate, and plants assimilate nitrate into proteins.

check.question: Which bacteria turn ammonium into nitrite, then nitrite into nitrate?
check.why: Nitrosomonas makes nitrite from ammonium; Nitrobacter then makes nitrate from nitrite.

content.heading: Denitrification and the cycle's use
paragraphs: After heavy rain, a waterlogged field loses nitrate even though fertiliser was added. Denitrifying bacteria in airless soil convert that nitrate back into nitrogen gas for the air. This return work is called denitrification, the opposite of nitrification.

Nitrification adds oxygen to nitrogen to build nitrate up in soil. Denitrification does the reverse by stripping oxygen away again. So nitrification feeds plants, while denitrification sends nitrogen back to the air.

Farmers add fertiliser to replace nitrate that crops remove and that rain washes away. Too much nitrate in water, called eutrophication, makes algae bloom and starves fish of oxygen. The cycle shows why fertiliser must be used with care.
bullets: Denitrifying bacteria release nitrogen gas, N2, from nitrate in airless soil.
Nitrification builds nitrate; denitrification destroys nitrate.
Fertiliser restores soil fertility but excess nitrate pollutes ponds and wells.
content.takeaway: Denitrification returns nitrogen to the air; careless fertiliser pollutes water.

check.question: Waterlogged soil loses nitrate as gas because
options: Denitrifying bacteria make nitrogen gas from nitrate
Plants absorb nitrate to make proteins
Lightning joins nitrogen and oxygen in air
check.why: In airless soil, denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate back into nitrogen gas.

visual.caption: Each step passes nitrogen on until denitrification returns it to the air.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When a question names a step, ask where nitrogen moves from and to. Fixation locks air nitrogen in, nitrification builds nitrate, assimilation builds protein, denitrification releases nitrogen gas again and again.

content.problem: A farm cycle is described: leaves rot to ammonium; Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter act; a plant builds protein; airless soil releases gas. Name the process at each stage.

steps.reason: Dead matter releases ammonium, but named cycle steps start after that
Nitrosomonas then Nitrobacter convert ammonium through nitrite to nitrate
steps.result: Nitrate is ready in soil water

steps.reason: Roots assimilate nitrate into protein; denitrators then release nitrogen gas
steps.result: Assimilation then denitrification complete the cycle

content.question: A soil sample has plenty of nitrogen gas but crops still grow poorly. Which cycle step is failing, and what would you check?
hints: Think about which step plants cannot start from nitrogen gas
Ask whether nitrifying bacteria have oxygen in the soil
Check if nitrate is being formed from ammonium

content.heading: Go deeper: Why fixation needs so much energy
paragraphs: Nitrogen gas looks harmless because two atoms share a triple bond. That bond holds the two atoms very tightly together. Breaking it takes a great deal of energy before anything useful can be made.

Lightning supplies that energy in one fierce flash. The heat splits nitrogen and oxygen molecules apart so they can join again as oxides. The new bonds need far less energy than the lost triple bond alone.

The Haber process feeds energy slowly with heat and pressure. At about 450 degrees, the iron catalyst opens the triple bond at a steady rate. Engineers accept lower yield so the reaction can run all day without huge cost.

Legume bacteria pay the energy bill with a different coin. The plant feeds them sugars that break down to release energy. Enzymes then use that trickle of energy to pry the triple bond open in cool soil.
That is why fixation is never free in the field. A power station burns fuel, a storm spends heat, and a bean spends leaf sugar. Each route pays the same bond-breaking price by a different method.
bullets: N≡N triple bond energy is about 941 kilojoules per mole.
Lightning works by sudden heat, not by steady pressure.
Haber uses heat, pressure and iron to balance speed and yield.
Rhizobium uses plant sugars and enzymes to work in cool soil.

content.heading: Go deeper: The two nitrification bacteria at work
paragraphs: Nitrification is not one step but two bacterial hands passing nitrogen on. The first hand belongs to Nitrosomonas. It feeds on ammonium and exhales nitrite into the soil water.
Nitrosomonas needs oxygen to do this work well. In loose, airy soil it grows fast and turns ammonium quickly. In waterlogged soil it slows down because oxygen is scarce, so ammonium may build up.
The second hand belongs to Nitrobacter. It catches the nitrite left by Nitrosomonas and adds oxygen again. The product is nitrate, which stays dissolved and travels to plant roots.

Nitrite rarely piles up because the two bacteria live side by side. Where one releases nitrite, the other soon consumes it. Accumulation marks broken cooperation, such as sudden fertiliser, cold soil or blocked air.
Farmers help these bacteria by tilling and draining the field. Loose soil lets oxygen reach their roots. Balanced fertiliser feeds them without flooding the soil with ammonium.

Exam questions name the pair in order because the order excuses the reason. NH4+ to NO2- is first, NO2- to NO3- is second. Reversing them suggests denitrification, which releases nitrogen gas instead.
bullets: Nitrosomonas: ammonium to nitrite; needs oxygen and moisture.
Nitrobacter: nitrite to nitrate; prefers airy soil.
Nitrite is toxic to seedlings when it piles up.
Both bacteria slow in waterlogged or very acid soil.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps that confuse the cycle
paragraphs: The commonest trap swaps fixation with nitrification. Fixation starts from nitrogen gas in air or soil air. Nitrification starts later, from ammonium already in the soil.

The next trap swaps nitrification with denitrification. Nitrification builds nitrate, so it feeds crops. Denitrification destroys nitrate and releases nitrogen gas, so it starves crops if it runs wild.

The third trap mixes nitrite and nitrate as if they were the same. Nitrite, NO2-, is the middle stage and is toxic when it builds up. Nitrate, NO3-, is the plant food form and the main pollutant when it leaches.

The fourth trap forgets that Haber and lightning are both fixation. An option that calls Haber nitrification fails, even if ammonia is named. Ask what the starting material is: nitrogen gas means fixation.

A safe solving habit is to trace one nitrogen atom through the question. Follow it from air to ammonia to nitrate to protein and back to air. If the atom cannot move as described, the answer is wrong.
Practice by sorting each new fact into its stage before you memorise its name. Stage decides the bacteria, the input and the output every time.
bullets: Fixation starts from N2 gas; nitrification starts from NH4+.
Nitrification builds nitrate; denitrification releases N2.
Nitrite is middle and toxic; nitrate is plant food.
Relevance: fertiliser restores fertility, excess nitrate pollutes water.

lessons.title: Iron from Sulphide Ores
lessons.objective: Determine the method of extraction of iron from sulphide ores, specify the properties and uses of the different forms of iron, and compare the advantages of steel over iron.

content.heading: Iron from sulphide ores
paragraphs: Iron can be won from two kinds of rock. Oxide ores go straight to the blast furnace. Sulphide ores must first be roasted, which burns off the sulphur and leaves an oxide the furnace can reduce.

content.heading: Roasting sulphide ores to oxides
paragraphs: A builder finds iron locked in yellow pyrite, FeS2, and in copper-iron chalcopyrite. These sulphide ores cannot go straight into the blast furnace because carbon reduces oxides, not sulphides. The ore must first change its chemistry.

Roasting means heating the crushed sulphide strongly in air. The sulphur burns away as sulphur dioxide and the iron becomes iron(III) oxide: 4FeS2 + 11O2 → 2Fe2O3 + 8SO2. Roasting is therefore oxidation, which gives the oxide the furnace needs.

The roasted oxide is now charged with limestone and coke. Hot air at the bottom burns coke to carbon monoxide, which reduces the oxide to molten iron. Limestone fluxes the impurities into slag, so each stage has its own job.
bullets: Sulphide ore: pyrite (FeS2) or chalcopyrite; roast it first.
Roasting: 4FeS2 + 11O2 → 2Fe2O3 + 8SO2; sulphide to oxide.
Blast furnace: carbon monoxide reduces oxide; limestone makes slag.
content.takeaway: Roasting converts sulphide to oxide; the furnace then reduces that oxide.

check.question: Why must pyrite be roasted before the blast furnace?
options: Iron is present as an oxide
Sulphide must become oxide for reduction
check.why: Carbon monoxide reduces oxides, so sulphide must first become oxide.

content.heading: Forms of iron and what each form is for
paragraphs: The furnace taps pig iron, the crude metal rich in carbon at about four percent. Pig iron is hard but so brittle that it shatters under a blow. It is rarely used directly because it feeds cast iron and steel.

Cast iron, made with less carbon, is hard and brittle for pipes, covers and cookware. Wrought iron is nearly pure, soft and tough for gates and chains that must bend without breaking. Tough resists breaking; brittle cracks.

Mild steel has little carbon, so it stays tough and weldable for beams, rails and car bodies. Stainless steel adds chromium and nickel for a rust-proof film on cutlery, sinks and medical tools. Carbon and alloying decide the form and its use.
bullets: Pig iron: about 4% carbon, brittle; feeds cast iron and steel.
Cast iron: hard, brittle; pipes, covers, cookware.
Wrought iron: nearly pure, tough; gates, chains. Mild steel: weldable; beams, rails.
Stainless steel: chromium and nickel; rust-proof; cutlery, sinks.
content.takeaway: Carbon content and alloying separate every form of iron.

check.question: A gate and a chain need a form of iron that is nearly pure, soft and tough. Which form fits?
check.why: Wrought iron is nearly pure iron, so it is soft and tough for bending.

content.heading: Why steel beats plain iron
paragraphs: Plain iron is soft and rusts quickly, so gates and beams soon fail. Steel keeps iron's low cost but gains strength and hardness from a small amount of carbon. That one change gives it far greater load-bearing power.

More carbon gives harder, stronger steel for tools, springs and rails that must keep an edge. Less carbon keeps mild steel tough and weldable for construction. Picking the carbon level is therefore picking the job.

Stainless steel adds chromium and nickel, so a thin film stops rust where plain iron fails. Steel therefore beats plain iron in strength, hardness, rust resistance and range of uses, from construction to surgery.
bullets: Strength and hardness: more carbon, higher strength; heat-treated for edges.
Rust resistance: stainless chromium film; plain iron rusts fast.
Range of uses: bridges, machines, vehicles, tools; wider than wrought or cast iron.
content.takeaway: Steel beats plain iron in strength, hardness, rust resistance and uses.

check.question: Which advantage lets steel hold a cutting edge that plain iron cannot?
options: More carbon with heat treatment for hardness
check.why: Steel's controlled carbon and heat treatment give hardness; pure iron is soft.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Roasting turns sulphide into oxide, carbon monoxide reduces that oxide, and limestone fluxes the impurities into slag. Do not swap roasting with reduction: roasting oxidises, reduction removes oxygen.

content.problem: Balance the roasting of pyrite: FeS2 + O2 → Fe2O3 + SO2.

steps.reason: Two irons on the right need two on the left
Four sulphurs on the left need four on the right
Right side has 3 + 8 = 11 oxygens, so O2 needs 5.5; multiply all by 2

content.question: Chalcopyrite must be turned into iron in the blast furnace. List the two chemical stages in order.
hints: Chalcopyrite is a sulphide, like pyrite
First roast in air to make the oxide
Then reduce the oxide with carbon monoxide in the furnace

content.heading: Go deeper: What roasting does to sulphur and iron
paragraphs: Roasting is burning, and it gives out heat. That heat helps the furnace, but the sulphur dioxide gas must be captured. In many plants the gas is cleaned and then used to make sulphuric acid, so a waste gas becomes a useful chemical.

The sulphur in pyrite is pushed to a higher oxidation state, while iron is also oxidised. Oxygen from the air is the oxidising agent, and the solid shrinks as sulphur leaves as gas. The remaining porous oxide is easy for carbon monoxide to attack.

Chalcopyrite raises a second problem because it holds copper as well as iron. Roasting alone does not separate those metals, so copper works must handle the roasted ore differently from a pyrite-only plant. JAMB asks about pyrite in plain terms, but the mixed ore is why chalcopyrite is named.

If roasting is skipped, sulphur stays in the iron and spoils it. Sulphur makes steel brittle and hard to weld, which is why the gas must leave before reduction begins. Roasting is therefore purification by oxidation, not merely heating.

The same logic explains why oxide ores need no roasting. Haematite already holds iron joined to oxygen, so it can go directly to reduction. Sulphide ore has the wrong partner atom, and roasting swaps sulphur for oxygen before reduction can start.
bullets: Roasting releases heat; sulphur dioxide may be captured for acid.
Iron and sulphur are oxidised; porous oxide reduces easily.
Chalcopyrite adds copper, so roasting alone does not win iron.

content.heading: Go deeper: How carbon turns one metal into many forms
paragraphs: Pure iron is soft because its crystal layers slide past each other. Carbon atoms jam those slides, so more carbon means harder and stronger metal. Past a point the jamming is so complete that the metal snaps instead of bending.

Pig iron at about four percent carbon is jammed almost completely, hence its brittleness. Cast iron keeps more carbon than steel but less than pig iron, so it casts well yet breaks under shock. Wrought iron has almost no carbon left, so it bends and welds.

Mild steel with less than about 0.3 percent carbon is the workhorse for construction because it is tough, cheap and weldable. Raising the carbon gives tool steel that holds an edge but is harder to weld. Each grade is a trade between toughness and hardness.

Stainless steel changes the surface, not just the bulk. Chromium forms a thin oxide film that re-forms after a scratch, which is why cutlery stays bright. Aluminium and zinc protect themselves the same way, so film protection is a general pattern, not an iron trick.

Heat treatment adds a final control. Quenching steel in water or oil locks in hardness, while tempering warms it to restore toughness. That is why two steels with the same carbon can still behave very differently after different cooling.
bullets: Carbon pins crystal slides: more carbon, harder, then brittle.
Mild steel under 0.3 percent carbon welds; tool steel holds edges.
Chromium film on stainless steel re-forms after a scratch.

content.heading: Go deeper: Traps that cost marks in iron questions
paragraphs: The first trap swaps roasting with reduction. Roasting adds oxygen to the ore, while reduction removes oxygen from the oxide. Any option that calls roasting a reduction reverses the chemistry and must be rejected at once.

The second trap names carbon as the reducer. Coke is fuel, but carbon monoxide does the reducing in the furnace. Limestone is neither fuel nor reducer; it is the flux that carries impurities into slag.

The third trap mixes wrought iron with cast iron. Wrought iron is nearly pure and tough, fit for gates and chains. Cast iron is hard and brittle, fit for pipes and covers. Toughness belongs to the purer metal, not the harder one.

The fourth trap reverses steelmaking. Oxygen in the converter burns carbon out of pig iron; it never adds carbon. Mild steel, high-carbon steel and stainless steel differ mainly in carbon level and alloy additions.

The last trap treats stainless steel as just harder mild steel. Its name points to rust resistance from chromium, not hardness alone. A question about sinks or cutlery that lists mild steel as the answer ignores that film.
bullets: Roasting is oxidation; reduction removes oxygen later.
Carbon monoxide reduces; carbon burns; limestone fluxes.
Wrought iron is tough; cast iron is brittle.

lessons.title: Alloys: Constituents and Uses
lessons.objective: Specify the constituents and uses of steel, stainless steel, brass, bronze, type-metal, duralumin, soft solder, permalloy and alnico, and compare alloys to pure metals.

content.heading: Alloys: constituents and uses
paragraphs: Pure metals are too soft or too weak for the job. An alloy mixes a metal with others so the blend is harder, stronger or safer. This lesson names the mixtures behind steel, brass, bronze, solder, magnets and aircraft parts.

content.heading: Iron alloys: steel, stainless steel and magnet alloys
paragraphs: Pure iron is too soft for beams and knives. Steel mixes iron with a little carbon, and the carbon pins the crystals. The blend is harder and stronger than pure iron, so it carries loads and holds edges.

Stainless steel adds chromium and nickel to iron. Its surface film blocks rust, so it suits cutlery, sinks and medical tools where strength alone would not suffice. Permalloy, iron with nickel, concentrates magnetism for relay and transformer cores, beating plain iron as a magnetic path.

Alnico mixes iron with aluminium, nickel, cobalt and copper. It keeps its magnetism without an outside supply, so it makes permanent magnets for motors and pickup cartridges. Each added element is the clue to the special job.
bullets: Steel: iron plus carbon; construction and tools; harder, stronger.
Stainless steel: iron, chromium, nickel; cutlery, sinks; rust-proof.
Permalloy: iron plus nickel; magnet cores; better magnetic path.
Alnico: iron, aluminium, nickel, cobalt, copper; permanent magnets.
content.takeaway: Carbon gives strength, chromium gives rust resistance, nickel and cobalt give magnetism.

check.question: A transformer core needs an iron alloy that concentrates magnetism. Which alloy fits?
check.why: Permalloy (iron plus nickel) is chosen for its magnetic properties.

content.heading: Copper and aluminium alloys for shape and lightness
paragraphs: Pure copper is soft, so it dents and wears too quickly for keys and bells. Brass mixes copper with zinc, and zinc hardens the blend while keeping its golden colour. That hardness and colour suit instruments, keys and decorative fittings.
Bronze mixes copper with tin, making hard, ringing metal that takes fine detail. Bells use its tone, medals and statues its hardness and patina. Tin turns soft copper into bell metal.

Duralumin mixes aluminium with copper, magnesium and manganese. It is far stronger than pure aluminium yet stays light, so it builds aircraft frames. The added metals supply strength while lightness is kept.
bullets: Brass: copper plus zinc; instruments, keys; harder, golden.
Bronze: copper plus tin; bells, medals; hard, ringing, detailed.
Duralumin: aluminium, copper, magnesium, manganese; aircraft; light, strong.
content.takeaway: Zinc hardens brass, tin rings bronze, and duralumin trades weight for strength.

check.question: A bell needs a copper alloy that rings well and takes fine detail. Which alloy is used?
check.why: Bronze is copper plus tin, chosen for its ringing tone and hardness.

content.heading: Soft alloys and the rule for alloys
paragraphs: Some alloys are wanted soft and low-melting, not strong. Type-metal mixes lead with antimony and tin, so it melts sharply and holds its shape for printing blocks. Pure lead is too soft and weak to hold type.

Soft solder mixes lead with tin, so it melts low and wets joints cleanly. A plumber can join pipes without melting them, which pure lead or tin alone cannot do well. Its low melting point is the advantage.
The rule is this: an alloy beats the pure metal for one job. It is usually harder, may resist rust or hold magnetism, and often melts over a range, not at one sharp point.
bullets: Type-metal: lead, antimony, tin; printing blocks; sharp melt, wear-proof.
Soft solder: lead plus tin; joining pipes; low melting, wetting joints.
Alloy rule: harder, stronger, or more resistant than the pure metal.
content.takeaway: Alloys gain one winning property over the pure metal for a chosen job.

visual.caption: Alloys are judged by the one property they improve over the pure metal.

check.question: Which statement correctly compares an alloy with its pure metal?
options: An alloy is a single element
An alloy melts at one sharp point always
An alloy is usually harder and stronger than the pure metal
An alloy is always softer than the pure metal
check.why: Alloys are mixtures that are usually harder, stronger, or more resistant than the pure metal.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Name the added metal first, then the job. Zinc in brass, tin in bronze and solder, chromium in stainless steel: the added element points to the property the alloy was made to gain.

content.problem: A bell metal is a copper alloy with tin that rings well. Name the alloy and state its advantage over pure copper.

steps.reason: Tin mixed with copper points to bronze, not brass
Pure copper is soft and dull, so bells and detail fail
steps.result: Pure copper too soft for bells

steps.reason: Tin hardens the blend and gives a ringing tone

content.question: A sink must stay rust-free and a transformer core must guide magnetism. Name the iron alloy for each job.
hints: Rust-free needs a chromium film on iron
Guiding magnetism needs iron with nickel for cores
Contrast stainless steel with permalloy for the two jobs

content.heading: Go deeper: Why mixing metals changes their hardness
paragraphs: In a pure metal the atoms sit in neat rows and the rows can slide. An added atom of a different size jams the slide, so the rows must push past a barrier to move. That jamming is felt outside the crystal as hardness.
