Carbon in steel is the classic jam, but zinc in brass and tin in bronze jam copper in the same way. The smaller the added atoms relative to the host, the stronger the pinning tends to be. Too much of the added metal, though, makes the blend brittle.

Hardness is not the only gain. Chromium in stainless steel does not mainly jam crystals; it skins the surface with an oxide film. Nickel in permalloy changes how magnetic domains move, not how crystals slide. Each additive writes a different property.

Melting also changes because the mixture has no single neat lattice. Pure lead melts sharply, while lead-tin solder softens gradually over a range. Type-metal, by contrast, is chosen to melt sharply so type fills moulds cleanly. The use decides whether a range or a point is wanted.

The exam rule follows: say the added metal, then the property it buys, then the use. A bare list of symbols without the property explains nothing. Properties are the bridge between constituents and uses.
bullets: Added atoms jam crystal slides, so alloys are harder to deform.
Film formers and magnetic additives work differently from hardeners.
Melting may sharpen or spread, depending on the mix and its use.

content.heading: Go deeper: Choosing the right alloy for the job
paragraphs: Brass and bronze are the pair candidates confuse because both are copper alloys with a golden colour. Zinc is the brass marker and tin is the bronze marker. Keys, instruments and door fittings point to brass, while bells, medals and statues point to bronze.

Steel and stainless steel share iron but diverge on rust. Mild steel wins on cost and weldability for beams and bodies, while stainless wins where water and air would ruin mild steel. A sink or cutlery made from mild steel would rust, so the film matters more than strength there.

Permalloy and alnico both contain iron and nickel, so they are confused on paper. Permalloy is soft magnetically and guides fields in cores, while alnico is a hard magnet that keeps its own field. Guide or keep is the discrimination question.

Soft solder and type-metal both rely on lead, but solder must melt low to join, while type-metal must melt sharply to cast. Tin in solder lowers the melting point for joining, while antimony in type-metal hardens lead for printing. Joining versus casting separates them.

Duralumin is the lightness answer because aluminium is about a third the weight of steel for the same volume. Its copper, magnesium and manganese additions restore strength that pure aluminium lacks. Where weight is penalised, duralumin wins over steel.
bullets: Brass has zinc; bronze has tin; keys versus bells.
Permalloy guides fields; alnico keeps its own magnetism.
Solder joins at low melt; type-metal casts type sharply.

content.heading: Go deeper: Traps that cost marks in alloy questions
paragraphs: The first trap swaps zinc and tin. Brass is copper plus zinc for instruments and keys, while bronze is copper plus tin for bells and medals. Any option pairing zinc with bells or tin with keys has crossed the markers.

The second trap forgets nickel in stainless steel or adds it to the wrong alloy. Stainless steel is iron with chromium and nickel, where chromium supplies the rust film. Duralumin is aluminium based and never contains iron as its main metal.

The third trap treats alnico and permalloy as the same magnet. Alnico makes permanent magnets because it holds magnetism alone, while permalloy is a core material that concentrates fields. One keeps a field, the other guides a field.

The fourth trap ignores melting behaviour. Soft solder is chosen for melting low, type-metal for melting sharply, and duralumin for lightness. A joint that needs low melting must not be answered with a high-carbon steel.

The final trap lists constituents without the gain. Every alloy item in JAMB expects the added metal, the property it buys and the use. Writing iron plus copper alone for duralumin, without magnesium and manganese, misses the alloy.
bullets: Zinc means brass; tin means bronze, solder and bells.
Chromium means rust-proof stainless steel; light means duralumin.
Guide a field: permalloy; keep a field: alnico.
